articles.content: A television drama no longer needs a television-sized screen, or even a half-hour episode. Microdramas — serialized stories filmed vertically and delivered in episodes often lasting a minute or two — are becoming a growing part of the streaming business. The format first took off in China , where producers condensed familiar soap opera plots — such as secret fortunes, time travel and long-awaited revenge — into episodes short enough to watch while waiting for a bus. The total amount of users of microdrama apps in China grew from 10 million to 400 million in three years . Microdrama platforms have developed a distinctive business model that sets them apart from traditional TV. Viewers can watch a handful of episodes before having to purchase virtual coins, subscribe or watch advertisements to unlock more. On DramaBox, for instance, viewers of Think Again! I’m the Hidden Boss Mom can watch the first 16 episodes free before paying for the remaining 36. Read more: TikTok’s popular microdramas shrink TV into bite-sized chunks The model has helped create a fast-growing industry . Microdramas generated US$11 billion worldwide in 2025 and are estimated to earn about US$14 billion in 2026. But the industry’s growth does not guarantee profitability. Industry and market research shows that while production costs are lower, attracting audiences is expensive, competition is intensifying and regulation remains unpredictable. How microdramas find their audiences Microdramas primarily rely on two distribution strategies . The first uses short teaser clips on TikTok or Instagram to attract viewers to dedicated apps, such as ReelShort and DramaBox, where they then pay to watch complete series. The second strategy involves distributing entire series through established video platforms, such as YouTube, where advertising revenue can support production. Microdramas generated more than 6.5 billion views on YouTube in the first half of 2026 . YouTube has also introduced the ability to group shorts into seasons and episodes , making serialized viewing easier within the platform. Other companies are trying to capitalize on existing audiences. In October, Tencent introduced Green Bubble, a free microdrama service integrated into its WeChat app. Users can discover series through search, links in a channel’s video feed or a section highlighting what their friends are watching. TikTok has also announced a partnership with a studio to produce microdramas . Its parent company, ByteDance, also operates Hongguo, a short-drama application that relies on algorithm-driven recommendations to attract viewers. How the business model works Microdrama platforms use several approaches to generate revenue. On DramaBox, viewers can subscribe, buy coins to unlock episodes or earn coins by watching ads . Green Bubble is free to watch and generates revenue through advertisements inserted into episodes. The payment structure is central to the format. Unlike a cinema ticket that provides access to an entire film or a streaming subscription that unlocks a catalogue, microdrama apps can charge viewers at particular moments in a story , often at cliffhangers when they are asked to pay to find out what happens next. This approach has raised consumer protection concerns. The consumer protection committee in the Chinese province of Jiangsu recorded 167,870 online complaints and other consumer-related reports concerning microdramas in the first half of 2024. Complaints included unclear charging and refund policies, misleading payment arrangements and difficulties cancelling subscriptions. Its investigation also found that some platforms did not clearly disclose the total cost of watching a series. Older consumers were particularly vulnerable to repeated purchases . Some companies are starting to use microdramas as advertising vehicles. American food company Bob Evans, for example, is releasing a 20-episode holiday series Christmas at Maple Hollow Inn through its own channels. Microdrama studio Pixie Studios integrates the company’s products into the story . High revenue doesn’t mean bigger profits Despite the market’s growth, the economic longevity of the industry remains an issue. Attracting viewers can be expensive, even when producing the shows themselves costs relatively little. FlexTV’s parent company, Mega Matrix, reported that advertising expenses accounted for 43 per cent of its total revenue in the first half of 2026 . Crazy Maple Studio, which runs ReelShort, nearly doubled its revenue in 2025 to 5.72 billion yuan, while its company-wide net loss was about 86 million yuan . Production costs are comparatively low. American streaming company Mansa produces microdramas on budgets from US$100,000 to US$250,000 per series . Low production costs allow producers to experiment with new ideas and take risks that would be difficult to justify with traditional TV budgets. But they also lower the barrier of entry for competitors, making it easier for rival studios to produce similar content. A Wall Street Journal segment about the microdrama boom. Artificial intelligence could push production costs down further. Kunlun Tech, which owns DramaWave, estimates it can make a microdrama series with AI for under US$20,000 , compared with $150,000 to $200,000 for a comparable series with human actors in dominant markets. AI-generated productions are already making an impact, with more than 94 per cent of new microdramas in China this year being AI-generated . At the end of October, 86 of the 100 titles on Hongguo’s trending chart were reportedly AI-made . As AI-generated content becomes more common, demand for some human performers and production workers will likely decline . What may strain the business model Hollywood studios and video platforms are feeling the pressure, and established streaming services and social platforms are increasingly adopting elements of the format. Omdia found that microdrama apps generate more daily viewing time than the biggest streaming platforms . Disney+ has added a vertical clip feed , HBO Max has begun testing one and YouTube now encourages creators to publish vertical series . Competition from established platforms could give microdramas access to larger audiences, but it also puts pressure on dedicated apps to differentiate their content and retain subscribers. Regulation is another area of uncertainty, particularly in China. China’s broadcast regulator recently launched a two-month campaign targeting eight types of content, including violent, sexually suggestive and wealth-flaunting material . Platform content moderation is also being tested, as Hongguo faces a lawsuit over the alleged unauthorized use of actress Zhao Liying’s likeness in AI-generated microdramas . Other alleged victims have said they are preparing legal action , so more disputes may follow. Recent Chinese regulations on microdramas require platforms offering paid content to clearly disclose pricing information and prohibit the use of algorithms designed to encourage addictive behaviour or excessive spending. In the United States, California requires businesses to obtain express consent to automatic renewal and lets customers who sign up online cancel online . Though a cliffhanger can get someone to watch one more episode, the hard test will always come in the end. Will viewers open the app again on their own, or will the company have to place an advertisement to reach them again? articles.content: Indigenous notions of relationality and reciprocity offer a way of understanding knowledge that goes beyond what technology can produce. (Wikimedia Commons/Thomas Melad) , CC BY-NC-ND Universities, long entrusted with teaching, research and knowledge production, are confronting one of their most significant challenges: The rising use of artificial intelligence . As AI technologies advance, they can perform tasks once considered the exclusive domain of humans. The implications extend beyond concerns about plagiarism and academic misconduct. As UNESCO has acknowledged , generative AI raises questions about the importance of human participation in knowledge production. For universities, these developments invite an uncomfortable question : If AI can produce knowledge more efficiently, what makes human contributions to knowledge production valuable? The changing nature of knowledge production Recent developments in mathematics demonstrate how consequential this question might be. In September 2026, OpenAI announced that an AI system had produced a proposed solution to one aspect of the Navier–Stokes Existence and Smoothness problem, one of mathematics’ celebrated Millennium Prize problems . The Navier-Stokes problem concerns the mathematical description of fluid motion and whether certain equations can produce solutions that become unbounded. Although formal recognition of the proposed solution is pending, the announcement represents a development in AI’s capacity to contribute to mathematical discovery. Read more: AI has solved a host of big maths problems – here’s why this threatens the whole field of mathematics Achievements like this may challenge assumptions about how knowledge is produced. AI can now produce mathematical proofs and generate original research across disciplines. Universities may therefore need to reconsider what distinguishes human intellectual contributions from those of AI. These concerns are not confined to mathematics. Research demonstrates that AI may complicate conventional approaches to academic assessment, authorship and integrity. However, responding to these developments primarily through regulation and restrictions risks overlooking a more important opportunity. Fundamentally, universities should reconsider the value they assign to human lived experience as a source of knowledge. Understanding lived experience Lived experience refers to the knowledge and understanding people develop through their encounters with the world. It encompasses more than simply having experiences. It involves interpreting those experiences, assigning meaning to them and drawing upon them to understand ourselves and others . Patrick O'Leary and Ming-sum Tsui , social work researchers from Australia and Hong Kong, emphasize the importance of recognizing lived experience as a source of expertise. They argue that lived experience contributes to meaningful relationships and professional practice. Their discussion offers an important insight for universities: Knowledge is not necessarily confined to information that can be collected, analyzed and reproduced . It can also emerge from the meanings people develop through participation in the world. This distinction is especially important when considering Onkwehón:we (Indigenous) understandings of knowledge. What universities can learn from Onkwehón:we For Onkwehón:we, (a Kanien’kehá term meaning “Original Peoples”), lived experience has long been central to understanding ourselves, our world and our responsibilities. Although Onkwehón:we knowledge traditions are diverse, many emphasize that knowledge emerges through relationships among people, communities and the natural world. Onkwehón:we scholarship on relationality demonstrates how knowledge and relationships are inseparable from the people and communities in which they are developed. From this perspective, lived experience is not exclusively individual in nature. It is also collective and intergenerational. It is shaped by language, ancestral knowledge and responsibilities to others. For Onkwehón:we, knowledge may be understood through participation in relationships that extend across generations. Learning from Elders and fulfilling responsibilities within communities are not merely opportunities to acquire information. They are experiences through which knowledge becomes meaningful. Research involving Indigenous communities in Canada illustrates how relationships with the land are informed by values of respect, responsibility and reciprocity. Reciprocity is the traditional value of balanced, respectful relations with each other and with the land. These understandings challenge the assumption that knowledge can be adequately evaluated outside of the relational and experiential contexts through which it is developed. Reaffirming the purpose of universities What can universities learn from Onkwehón:we perspectives as AI becomes increasingly potent? One possibility is to place greater emphasis on lived experience within teaching, learning and research. Read more: It’s taken thousands of years, but Western science is finally catching up to Traditional Knowledge Rather than evaluating learning primarily through written work, universities could place greater emphasis upon experiential learning and community engagement. These approaches can show how knowledge shapes relationships and responsibilities. Some faculties of education, such as at Wilfrid Laurier University , already use them in parts of their programming. This would not require abandoning AI. Nor would it suggest that Indigenous knowledge traditions exist simply to resolve problems facing universities. Rather, universities can recognize that human knowledge cannot be fully understood through technology alone. Onkwehón:we scholarship already challenges universities to reconsider how their disciplinary traditions privilege certain forms of knowledge while marginalizing relational and experiential ways of knowing. Artificial intelligence makes this reconsideration increasingly urgent. An example of how scientific orientations may be reconsidered is found in the study of time. A recent study on Onkwehón:we perspectives on time explores how scientific understandings of time may be enriched by Onkwehón:we lived experiences, including seasonal cycles and relationships with the Land. Such perspectives can broaden how universities approach scientific knowledge by connecting abstract concepts with human experience. The more consequential question concerns what universities believe knowledge is for and what responsibilities accompany its creation. Onkwehón:we understandings of lived experience offer a valuable starting point. They remind us that knowledge is not simply something we produce or possess. It is also something we live, share and carry through our relationships with others . As AI begins to transform how knowledge is produced, universities have an opportunity to reaffirm the importance of human experience. Rather than an alternative to intellectual achievement, it’s an essential part of what makes knowledge meaningful. Frank Deer receives funding from the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council of Canada.

articles.content: “The only way we’re gonna get through this,” Lucia tells Jason in Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA6), “is by sticking together.” GTA6 is, unlike its predecessors, built around a relationship between two lead characters. The game tracks their level of intimacy on a four-point scale : running on empty , partners in crime , crazy in love and hot together . As a player, you must actively maintain the bond between them — by having them be nice to each other, go on dates and of course work together to commit crimes. And yes, they even have sex. The game has a relationship meter that allows players to watch the connection between the two rise and fall. Rob Nelson, Rockstar North’s head of development, told The Verge : “You can still play it the old way, you can reject all of this stuff. But for people who do engage, it’s meaningful — you’re earning it, you’re working at it, just like in a normal relationship.” For some people, this idea, that a video game is trying to simulate a normal human relationship, will immediately set off alarm bells about the dangers of digital intimacy, especially for teenagers. I don’t think there is much to worry about. GTA6 is an immersive experience, to be sure, and players are definitely going to become invested in Lucia and Jason’s romance. But their interactions are scripted. Will artificial intimacy diminish us? Recently we have heard lots of dire warnings about what MIT researcher Sherry Turkle calls “artificial intimacy.” Turkle has recently published a book warning about the risks of emotional connections with artificial entities . In it, she says: “If these are the relationships we choose, we will be left in a world of non-relationships. Artificial intimacy is positioned to colonize and diminish the human kind.” Governments are also increasingly concerned about the risks of AI companionship, particularly for minors. China has prohibited AI companions for underage users. In the United States, several states have passed laws restricting or banning AI companions. U.S. congress is considering a federal law that would prohibit minors from using them. Tens of millions of people, including, inevitably, many teenagers, will play GTA6 in the coming months, and will experience first-hand the artificial intimacy between Jason and Lucia. They will spend hours deliberately fostering and building that intimacy. Should we be worried? A game that encourages empathy Turkle is mostly concerned about AI companions that engage users in open-ended conversations and respond directly to their emotional needs. These bots can create the impression of a reciprocal relationship with a partner who is responsive and emotionally invested. That’s a very different experience from developing a relationship between two fictional characters within a game. Also, GTA6 offers a notably positive vision of romance. Turkle argues that digital technologies allow us to experience the comforts of companionship without having to face up to the demands of human relationships. She argues that artificial intimacy is too easy, and this turns us off the messiness that comes with real attachment. GTA6 models something different. Jason and Lucia have to nurture their bond. They must talk to each other and be attentive to each other’s needs. Lucia reminds Jason: “Relationships are about communication, Jay.” And because players can switch between characters, they experience the relationship from both sides. As Rob Nelson, one of the three creative leads on GTA6 at Rockstar North, told The Guardian : “We’ve tried for the first time in a GTA to provide mechanisms that encourage empathy — for those who want it.” Arguably, Lucia and Jason show us just the sort of relationship that Turkle believes is threatened by technology. A transactional logic Though we definitely shouldn’t panic about GTA6’s digital intimacy, I do think there are aspects of the relationship that are worth noticing. The game is built around optimization. Players raise the couple’s bond meter through specific actions and the rewards are concrete. As the meter rises, the couple holds hands and kisses. At the top tier, the game unlocks the option for sex. Affection is a score, and intimacy becomes something the player earns by supplying the right inputs. Once the meter is maxed out, the couple never fights. In this way, it reproduces the sort of transactional logic that worries many critics of AI companions. In the game, these things are pretty harmless. The relationship is between two fictional characters, rather than between a user and a machine that claims to care about them. And no one profits from how attached the player becomes to Lucia or Jason. But the dynamic parallels some of the ways AI companion apps operate, and these can be more insidious. With these apps, the equivalent mechanics — reminders that your companion misses you, intimate content that is unlocked through engagement or by paying — are central to the business model. The laws of virtual romance As we debate whether and how to regulate AI companionship, the lesson here is not to target an entire class of technology. Blanket bans on AI companions are not the answer. Artificial intimacy can be harmless, or even positive, for users . Rather, we should focus on specific design features that can cause harm, particularly to young people. We should, for instance, look at the way AI companion apps are designed to maximize engagement, the way they use emotional pressure as a retention tactic and the way they present affection and sex as a reward for specific behaviours. Jason and Lucia are poised to become the digital world’s two most famous outlaws. It would be a nice irony if they end up teaching us a lesson about how to write better laws governing virtual romance. And no one profits from how attached the player becomes to Lucia or Jason. But the dynamic parallels some of the ways AI companion apps operate, and these can be more insidious. With these apps, the equivalent mechanics — reminders that your companion misses you, intimate content that is unlocked through engagement or by paying — are central to the business model. The laws of virtual romance As we debate whether and how to regulate AI companionship, the lesson here is not to target an entire class of technology. Blanket bans on AI companions are not the answer. Artificial intimacy can be harmless, or even positive, for users . Rather, we should focus on specific design features that can cause harm, particularly to young people. We should, for instance, look at the way AI companion apps are designed to maximize engagement, the way they use emotional pressure as a retention tactic and the way they present affection and sex as a reward for specific behaviours. Jason and Lucia are poised to become the digital world’s two most famous outlaws. It would be a nice irony if they end up teaching us a lesson about how to write better laws governing virtual romance. articles.content: How much public support does a company need before it can build a major development in a community? And who gets to decide if that threshold is met? These questions are emerging in New Brunswick, where two communities are approaching the prospect of AI data centre development differently. In Fundy Shores, the mayor has called for new rules governing AI data centres , even though no developer has proposed building one in his municipality yet. The municipality wants future data centre developers to obtain council approval through a rezoning process, giving residents an opportunity to weigh in before construction could proceed. In nearby Saint John, residents have been debating a proposed facility in Lorneville . At a public meeting, they raised concerns about air quality, water consumption and the benefits such a project would bring. After the meeting, one resident told reporters: “I think it demonstrates that there is no social licence for this project.” The two communities illustrate different points in the debate over social license: how to establish public support for a project before it is proposed, and what happens when residents believe that support is absent. As an environmental communication researcher, I have studied how supporters and opponents of liquefied natural gas development in British Columbia made competing claims about whose interests those projects would serve. I see similar disputes in debates over AI data centres, particularly when different parties claim to speak for the people who will live alongside a project. What is a social licence? Having a “social licence to operate” refers to the ongoing acceptance of a project by people affected by it . The term emerged in the mining industry in the 1990s, when companies recognized that even with government permits in hand, opposition from neighbours could delay or disrupt their operations. It captured the practical importance of public support, though it left open who could grant it or judge when it had been lost. Unlike a government permit, a social licence is not a formal legal authorization. It’s an informal relationship between a developer and the communities affected by its activities. Consider the debate over Enbridge’s proposed Northern Gateway pipeline . In April 2014, residents of Kitimat, B.C., where the pipeline was proposed to terminate, voted on the project. Of those who voted, 58.4 per cent opposed it . Read more: Where does all the hardware go? The hidden environmental footprint of AI data centres What followed was a political dispute about how much weight residents’ responses should carry . Opponents pointed to that result as evidence that Enbridge had failed to earn local acceptance. An idea the mining industry had used to explain why companies needed public support had given residents a way to express their opposition. Some pipeline advocates, including newspaper columnists and Conservative politicians, objected that opponents were claiming a veto over projects of national importance. A company could welcome consultation, yet disagree about what should happen when residents rejected its proposal. Whose support counts? Claims that a project has or lacks a social licence often depend on who is speaking for the community, and whose views are being counted. The public meeting in Saint John gave some residents a chance to voice their concerns, but it could not establish how the wider community felt about the proposal. The same challenge arises when projects are presented as having public support. A council resolution reflects elected representatives’ positions; a benefits agreement records what its signatories accepted while a public vote reflects the views of those who participated. Each provides evidence about a different group of people , but none necessarily represents everyone affected. This question of representation is especially important when projects affect Indigenous nations. First Nations, Inuit and Métis communities have distinct rights, governing institutions and authority to make decisions. Their views cannot be subsumed into municipal consultation or treated as another measure of local opinion. What if a community changes its mind? There is a danger to treating social licence as a one-time decision, as I mentioned in a recent interview about Fundy Shores . Before a data centre is constructed, residents have forecasts and promises to consider. Once a facility opens, they can measure those promises against their lived experiences, including how the operator responds when something goes wrong. Sherbrooke, Que., offers one example of how the experience of a project after it opens can change how a community views it. The city agreed to supply electricity to Bitfarms for a bitcoin mining facility . Soon after it opened, neighbours began complaining to the city about the noise. Bitfarms replaced the fans and installed a noise barrier, but the problem persisted. In 2021, the city and the company agreed in principle to move the operation to an industrial park . A social licence, then, is not something a developer keeps indefinitely. It largely depends on whether a project continues to meet the expectations of the people affected by it. Residents views may change as a project develops and its impacts become clearer. A council’s approval may allow construction to proceed, but it does not guarantee lasting community acceptance. Residents must have opportunities to hold operators accountable as they experience the project’s effects. articles.content: Aging can seem like a negative process, one that causes our bodies to slow down and deteriorate. The aging brain, however, retains remarkable resilience. And some of the changes that occur within the aging brain are actually helpful adaptations. Our recent research study reveals this process of adaptation — showing that the brains of healthy older adults may cope better with lack of sleep than those of younger adults . Neuroplasticity in older age In this study, we investigated the neuroplasticity of human brain networks across the lifespan. Neuroplasticity refers to the brain’s extraordinary ability to change , particularly through the reorganization of brain connections. The most extreme periods of neuroplasticity occur during brain development in childhood , adolescence and the transition to early adulthood . However, the healthy brain retains its neuroplasticity throughout the lifespan, and undergoes periods of pronounced reorganization even in older age . Aging brains face many challenges, including cortical thinning or brain shrinkage , white matter demyelination and cognitive decline . As a result, many researchers treat aging as a proxy for purely negative brain changes. Our research goes against this trend by identifying multiple ways in which brain changes may actually be helpful adaptations to the challenges of aging. Preserving function for tomorrow Previous research has suggested that older adults do not suffer as badly from the negative effects of minimal sleep — decreased cognitive ability and mood — as younger adults do. In our study, we wanted to understand what is happening in the brain to cause this. So we compared the brains of younger adults (20-30 years) and older adults (65-75 years) after experiencing a full night of sleep and a night with only three hours of sleep. We found that part of the older brain’s functional connectivity responded in the opposite way to the brains of younger adults. After a night with only three hours of sleep, older adult brains reduced connections in a way that increased modularity . That is, their brain regions formed more local modules, with a small number of global connections between modules. Conversely, younger adult brains showed decreased modularity . Modularity is an efficient network organization associated with better cognitive outcomes . Our research suggests the brain may compensate for age-related changes by responding to short-term sleep loss in an adaptive way, preserving efficient brain function the next day. Strengthening local connections These findings complement our broader program of research identifying long-term reorganizations of brain networks that support cognitive outcomes in older age. Interestingly, these are distinct from the connectivity patterns that are beneficial for younger adults. We continue to see a recurring theme: The healthy brain seems to adapt to white matter demyelination with age by relying less on longer global connections and instead strengthening local connectivity . This growing program of research speaks to the healthy aging brain’s resilience to challenges, where neuroplasticity supports reorganization and adaptation. Sleep while you are young How do we help to promote these neuroplastic adaptations? One way is through physical activity . Another important lifestyle factor is getting a healthy amount of sleep throughout one’s life . Recent research has shown that sleep can directly affect both the risk of Alzheimer’s disease and how quickly it progresses . The amyloid and tau proteins that accumulate in brains with Alzheimer’s disease accumulate at a faster rate when sleep is disrupted . Researchers estimate that 15 per cent of Alzheimer’s disease cases could be prevented by identifying people with poor sleep quality and intervening to promote better sleep. The disease processes that cause Alzheimer’s disease develop for decades before an individual will experience memory loss and be diagnosed with dementia , so there is a large window of opportunity to detect and treat the disease and prevent cognitive decline. For some, sleep is an important treatment target. Brianne Kent receives funding from CIHR, NSERC, Canada Research Chairs, Michael Smith Health Research BC, and Canada Foundation for Innovation. articles.content: A new day, a new cyberattack. The most recent is an attack that impacted 178 major websites, including those of the BBC, CNN, Zoom, HSBC, Salesforce and Equifax . This follows a series of cyberattacks and disruptions over the last two months — most notably on supermarkets throughout Europe. A series of attacks in France during October raised refrigerator and freezer temperatures to 50 C in more than 350 supermarkets. Overnight, large amounts of food spoiled, equipment overheated and fires were reported. Affected stores had to discard food and temporarily close. Similar attacks and disruptions were then reported across several countries in November, including Ireland, Sweden, the Netherlands, Belgium, Estonia, Finland and Luxembourg. In all of these cases, hackers remotely reprogrammed internet-connected temperature controls. They switched evaporators to defrost mode, raising temperatures beyond safety limits. These simple changes impacted physical equipment, businesses and people. How will the next cyberattack unfold, and where? Our industrial critical infrastructure offers many targets — from blood banks to chemical manufacturing plants , nuclear reactors , aviation and other transportation systems and wastewater treatment facilities . The potential consequences are vast. Our team at the Cyber Security Evaluation and Assurance (CyberSEA) research lab at Carleton University has simulated cyberattacks on a Canadian municipal wastewater treatment facility to identify the most serious consequences. We have also mapped out seven dimensions for understanding cyberattack impacts . The vulnerability of critical infrastructure Critical infrastructure refers to 10 broad sectors including energy and utilities, water, health, transportation and food. Systems in these sectors provide essential services. Connecting the systems to the internet improves efficiency, but can also expose such services to modern cybersecurity threats. Cybersecurity analysis tends to focus on attacks and how they could have been prevented. Cyberattack impact analysis , on the other hand, looks at what happens after a system is compromised — which operations are disrupted, how the effects spread and who or what might be harmed. A supermarket is more than its refrigerator temperature controls. It’s a system involving food, equipment, employees, customers, business continuity and public confidence. Similarly, a water utility contains pumps and software but also protects a wider system of treatment processes, public health, the environment and access to safe water. Cyberattacks on critical infrastructure radiate impact through all of our lives. Learning from wastewater systems Wastewater treatment provides a good example of the far-reaching consequences of a cyberattack. When we simulated cyberattacks on a Canadian municipal wastewater treatment facility , we found this could force equipment to operate excessively or near safety limits. It could also increase chemical consumption, push the plant into costly contingency modes or interfere with chemical dosing. The most serious scenario involved discharging under-treated wastewater into the city’s river. This might seem extreme, but something similar has already happened. In 2000, a former employee attacked the Maroochy Shire wastewater system in Australia . He remotely interfered with sewage pumping stations, preventing pumps and alarms from operating properly. Over three months, millions of gallons of untreated sewage entered waterways and local parks. 7 dimensions of impact Our recent research identifies seven dimensions for understanding the consequences of cyberattacks. The supermarket attacks across Europe illustrate all seven. Operational impacts occur when a system cannot perform its intended function, while physical impacts involve changes or damage to equipment and materials. In the supermarkets, altered temperature controls disrupted food preservation, equipment overheated and food spoiled. The consequences can then spread beyond the system. Safety impacts expose people to hazards, such as fires or unsafe food. Environmental impacts harm air, water, land or ecosystems — such as discarded food creating additional waste. Economic impacts include lost products, equipment repairs, downtime and lost customers. Broader consequences may also emerge. Societal impacts disrupt communities or their access to important goods and services, such as fresh food. Reputational impacts arise when people lose confidence in an organization or service, for example, due to concerns about food safety. These dimensions are connected. One disrupted operation can produce several impacts at once, some continuing after the technical problem has been resolved. Preparing for consequences We may not know how the next cyberattack will unfold. But we can prepare for unsafe water, damaged equipment, environmental harm, interrupted services, financial losses and diminished public trust. Impact analysis helps decision-makers ask practical questions: Which consequences are unacceptable? Where are additional safeguards needed? Who must respond when safety or environmental harm occurs? Which services must be restored first? The goal is not merely to keep attackers out of computer systems. It is to keep essential services working when cyber-defences fail. articles.content: Google recently announced that its AI tools, including Gemini and Gemini Notebook, would be turned off by default for kindergarten to Grade 12 student accounts starting in early 2027. Google Search, its popular search engine, would also be turned off by default. The New York Times reported that Chris Phillips, vice president for education at Google, said: “Search and A.I. are deeply integrated,” and that if a school has banned A.I. , “they will not have access to search.” This means schools that want students to simply search on Google will have to accept Google’s AI whether they want it or not. As researchers who study education policy and technology, we see Google’s move as a wake-up call. It exposes how much power one company holds over schools, and why Canadian governments working with school boards, teacher unions and parents need to set the terms for how AI enters classrooms. Setting common regulatory standards at the federal and provincial levels could give schools the collective leverage they currently lack when dealing with trillion-dollar companies like Google . Read more: The release of AI chatbots has harmed teens’ learning and Canada needs to act How did we get here? Google presents the change as giving schools more control amid pushback from child-safety advocates, parents and educators after it switched on Gemini by default in Google Classroom for many K-12 students in August. Google Classroom is an online platform where teachers post assignments and students submit their work. Google has also said AI in its search function will guide students through problems step by step rather than give them quick answers. But guided or not, AI remains built in. Over the past 15 years, Google has become one of the largest providers of digital infrastructure to schools around the world largely by offering its tools for free or at low cost — although researchers highlight hidden costs in the form of data trails left exposed by privacy loopholes . Google’s ‘ecosystem’ Its influence comes not simply from selling individual products to schools, but from embedding schools within an interconnected ecosystem of software applications such as Google Classroom, hardware like Chromebooks and cloud-based services like Google Drive — all increasingly relied upon by schools. About 150 million students and teachers worldwide now use Google Classroom while 60 per cent of all Chromebook purchases are for use in education. This ecosystem approach gives Google immense leverage over schools. Even when offered a “choice,” schools cannot simply switch away from Google overnight. Switching to alternatives involves not only purchasing new software and hardware but also migrating data, retraining teachers and students and disrupting established routines and practices. Google’s decision to tie Search to AI shows how this dependence can become a form of coercion. ‘Pipeline of future users’ Although Google presents its investments in education as altruistic and benign , its commercial interests have always been central to its strategy. Internal company documents, filed in a U.S. lawsuit against Google and other social media companies, describe Google’s work in schools as building a “pipeline of future users.” A Google spokesperson said the documents “mischaracterize our work.” Read more: We street-proof our kids. Why aren’t we data-proofing them? Google Search, the company’s biggest revenue-generating business , lies at the core of that pipeline. As AI chatbots like OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Anthropic’s Claude gain popularity as alternatives to traditional internet search , they threaten not only Google’s current user base but also its future one. A generation that learns to access information online without “Googling” as its primary gateway is what Google wants to prevent. Seen from this lens, it’s no surprise Google isn’t letting schools search on Google without AI features embedded in one form or another. Who is setting the rules? This conundrum facing schools raises a central question: who sets the direction and conditions for AI in K-12 education? The Council of Ontario Directors of Education’s 2026 “AI in Education” resource cautions that students and staff are already using AI “in the absence of guidance.” Read more: Should AI chatbots simulate care for students? Alberta teachers say no For the 2026-27 school year, the Ontario education ministry required “Cyber Safety and Artificial Intelligence” to be one of four mandatory topics on teachers’ professional activity days, which includes getting familiar with AI tools. British Columbia has published a set of considerations to help school districts select AI tools. But it sets no rules of its own, leaving individual districts to make their own decisions. This approach assumes districts have meaningful choices. But Google sets the same terms for all schools, and changes them when it chooses. At the federal level, the emphasis has been more on AI adoption. In September, the federal government launched a $13-million National AI Literacy Initiative , in partnership with the Alberta Machine Intelligence Institute, that includes free, self-paced modules that show K-12 educators how to integrate AI into curriculum, assessment and teaching. The Canadian Teachers’ Federation has warned that the initiative puts “adoption before safety,” encouraging teachers to bring AI into classrooms before its safety and educational benefits can be established. Regulatory standards needed Google’s ultimatum shows why a human-centred approach to AI in education must begin with a fundamental question: Who gets to decide whether and how AI enters classrooms? Such an approach prioritizes students’ needs, rights and learning and teachers’ professional judgment over technology companies’ commercial interests. UNESCO’s guidance on generative AI in education points in this direction, setting out distinct responsibilities for governments, AI providers and users. Researchers have argued AI should be regulated through a developmental lens before it enters K-12 classrooms, and there is already evidence of why such safeguards are warranted. Read more: School board social media lawsuits: For too long we’ve sought individual solutions to a collective problem In July 2026, Common Sense Media gave the AI features in Google Search its lowest possible rating, “ unacceptable risk ,” after finding that they completed students’ homework assignments and failed to respond appropriately to children in crisis. Google disputed the findings , saying the testing relied on “a narrow set of ambiguous and contrived queries.” Questions about whether these tools are safe for children shouldn’t be settled by school boards alone. Setting joint standards allows school boards to weigh the educational value of AI against other pressing priorities, rather than treating its adoption as inevitable in already underfunded education systems . articles.description: Google recently announced that its AI tools, including Gemini and Gemini Notebook, would be turned off by default for kindergarten to Grade 12 student accounts starting in early 2027. Google Search, its popular search engine, would also be turned off by default. The New York Times reported that Chris Phillips, vice president for education at Google, said: “Search and A.I. are deeply integrated,” and that if a school has banned A.I. , “they will not have access to search.” This means schools that want students to simply search on Google will have to accept Google’s AI whether they want it or not. As researchers who study education policy and technology, we see Google’s move as a wake-up call. It exposes how much power one company holds over schools, and why Canadian governments working with school boards, teacher unions and parents need to set the terms for how AI enters classrooms. Setting common regulatory standards at the federal and provincial levels could give schools the collective leverage they currently lack when dealing with trillion-dollar companies like Google . Read more: The release of AI chatbots has harmed teens’ learning and Canada needs to act How did we get here? Google presents the change as giving schools more control amid pushback from child-safety advocates, parents and educators after it switched on Gemini by default in Google Classroom for many K-12 students in August. Google Classroom is an online platform where teachers post assignments and students submit their work. Google has also said AI in its search function will guide students through problems step by step rather than give them quick answers. But guided or not, AI remains built in. Over the past 15 years, Google has become one of the largest providers of digital infrastructure to schools around the world largely by offering its tools for free or at low cost — although researchers highlight hidden costs in the form of data trails left exposed by privacy loopholes . Google’s ‘ecosystem’ Its influence comes not simply from selling individual products to schools, but from embedding schools within an interconnected ecosystem of software applications such as Google Classroom, hardware like Chromebooks and cloud-based services like Google Drive — all increasingly relied upon by schools. About 150 million students and teachers worldwide now use Google Classroom while 60 per cent of all Chromebook purchases are for use in education. This ecosystem approach gives Google immense leverage over schools. Even when offered a “choice,” schools cannot simply switch away from Google overnight. Switching to alternatives involves not only purchasing new software and hardware but also migrating data, retraining teachers and students and disrupting established routines and practices. Google’s decision to tie Search to AI shows how this dependence can become a form of coercion. ‘Pipeline of future users’ Although Google presents its investments in education as altruistic and benign , its commercial interests have always been central to its strategy. Internal company documents, filed in a U.S. lawsuit against Google and other social media companies, describe Google’s work in schools as building a “pipeline of future users.” A Google spokesperson said the documents “mischaracterize our work.” Read more: We street-proof our kids. Why aren’t we data-proofing them? Google Search, the company’s biggest revenue-generating business , lies at the core of that pipeline. As AI chatbots like OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Anthropic’s Claude gain popularity as alternatives to traditional internet search , they threaten not only Google’s current user base but also its future one. A generation that learns to access information online without “Googling” as its primary gateway is what Google wants to prevent. Seen from this lens, it’s no surprise Google isn’t letting schools search on Google without AI features embedded in one form or another. Who is setting the rules? This conundrum facing schools raises a central question: who sets the direction and conditions for AI in K-12 education? The Council of Ontario Directors of Education’s 2026 “AI in Education” resource cautions that students and staff are already using AI “in the absence of guidance.” Read more: Should AI chatbots simulate care for students? Alberta teachers say no For the 2026-27 school year, the Ontario education ministry required “Cyber Safety and Artificial Intelligence” to be one of four mandatory topics on teachers’ professional activity days, which includes getting familiar with AI tools. British Columbia has published a set of considerations to help school districts select AI tools. But it sets no rules of its own, leaving individual districts to make their own decisions. This approach assumes districts have meaningful choices. But Google sets the same terms for all schools, and changes them when it chooses. At the federal level, the emphasis has been more on AI adoption. In September, the federal government launched a $13-million National AI Literacy Initiative , in partnership with the Alberta Machine Intelligence Institute, that includes free, self-paced modules that show K-12 educators how to integrate AI into curriculum, assessment and teaching. The Canadian Teachers’ Federation has warned that the initiative puts “adoption before safety,” encouraging teachers to bring AI into classrooms before its safety and educational benefits can be established. Regulatory standards needed Google’s ultimatum shows why a human-centred approach to AI in education must begin with a fundamental question: Who gets to decide whether and how AI enters classrooms? Such an approach prioritizes students’ needs, rights and learning and teachers’ professional judgment over technology companies’ commercial interests. UNESCO’s guidance on generative AI in education points in this direction, setting out distinct responsibilities for governments, AI providers and users. Researchers have argued AI should be regulated through a developmental lens before it enters K-12 classrooms, and there is already evidence of why such safeguards are warranted. Google disputed the findings , saying the testing relied on “a narrow set of ambiguous and contrived queries.” Questions about whether these tools are safe for children shouldn’t be settled by school boards alone. Setting joint standards allows school boards to weigh the educational value of AI against other pressing priorities, rather than treating its adoption as inevitable in already underfunded education systems . articles.content: Medications like Ozempic and Wegovy, which contain semaglutide — a GLP‑1 receptor agonist that helps regulate blood sugar, appetite and body weight — have become household names and important pillars in obesity management for the medical profession. Research has shown GLP-1 medications reduce body weight by an average of 15 per cent when used weekly for 68 weeks and combined with lifestyle interventions. This is because semaglutide acts on the brain to increase the feeling of fullness and to decrease appetite. These medications don’t work the same way for everyone, however. Our multidisciplinary research team at the University of Alberta is working to improve obesity care for people of all ages and to understand why some people respond better to semaglutide than others, and how their weight loss can be maintained over time. We are investigating the role of energy metabolism as a potentially important piece in a complex puzzle. The challenge of metabolic adaptation Research has shown semaglutide medications to improve quality of life , blood markers such as sugar or cholesterol , strength and overall health. Weight loss is only one measure of how well they work. We are exploring whether people’s responses to these medications could lie in individual factors such as genetics, metabolism, body composition, lifestyle, microbiota, associated diseases, age and sex. Obesity medication is an important pillar of obesity management and should be monitored as part of a comprehensive, multidisciplinary approach to care. (Obesity Canada) , CC BY-NC-ND Energy metabolism may also be an important piece of this puzzle. This is a measure of the total calories consumed (in) and the total calories burned (out). We burn calories all the time: for vital processes like breathing and thinking, physical activities like going to the gym and the everyday act of digesting food. When we lose weight, our bodies naturally need less energy. But sometimes, the body goes into an extra “energy-saving mode,” burning even fewer calories than we would expect. This is called metabolic adaptation, or adaptive thermogenesis . Think of it like a light bulb that automatically dims to save electricity. This is one reason why losing weight can become more difficult over time, sometimes leading to a weight-loss plateau. Emerging areas of research Changes in body weight and composition (the amount of fat and fat-free mass in our bodies) play an important role in energy metabolism. Both fat and fat-free mass use energy, even when we are resting. As we lose these tissues, our bodies naturally burn fewer calories. Researchers are still trying to understand whether weight-loss medications influence these processes differently. If we can understand how our bodies use energy during and after weight loss, this could help us develop better strategies for maintaining weight loss over the long term. We published a recent review of studies investigating the effects of GLP-1 therapies on energy utilization . We found a few studies exploring how semaglutide affects resting energy use, with findings that were neutral or inconclusive. The question of how semaglutide impacts energy use is an emerging area of study, and remains an open question for exploration. Personalized approaches to obesity At the University of Alberta, we have a gold-standard method to measure energy utilization called a whole-room indirect calorimeter . This is a rare research facility and is similar to a hotel suite that can precisely measure each component of energy use . This room can isolate the effects of changes in someone’s calorie burning at rest, after eating and during exercise. We are currently recruiting research participants with blood sugar regulation issues, such as insulin resistance or diabetes, who are about to start semaglutide treatment. We will follow their weight loss journey over six months to investigate changes in body weight and composition, and energy utilization using sophisticated approaches. Understanding how semaglutide influences energy use and body composition, and how these changes interact, could be an important step toward explaining why individuals respond differently to weight-loss treatment. This will allow us to contribute to more personalized approaches to obesity and Type 2 diabetes management in the future. Having a better understanding of how energy use changes with semaglutide-induced weight loss will also help us to better anticipate potential non-responders (people who do not lose weight) and offer alternative treatments sooner in their health journey. Lifestyle changes for success Importantly, current evidence suggests that if you are taking semaglutide or considering starting treatment, you should make a few lifestyle changes. Current guidelines recommend people using GLP-1 medications to engage in resistance exercise to optimize their body composition for the best results. (Obesity Canada) , CC BY-NC-ND These include improving your nutrition by increasing protein intake and prioritizing fresh foods , such as fruits, vegetables, whole grains, lean proteins like fish and poultry , nuts and seeds. It’s important to eat small portions at consistent times throughout the day, avoid skipping meals, pay attention to your hunger and fullness cues and choose water as your beverage of choice. It’s also recommended to engage in resistance exercise to support muscle and bone health and achieve the best results. These strategies may help limit reductions in energy use as the weight comes off. articles.content: Bell Canada’s AI Fabric data centre near Regina, Sask., has been touted as the “single largest private-sector capital investment” in Canadian history . Bell Canada says the project will use energy responsibly “without competing for local power resources.” But local residents have expressed concerns about the project’s potential water and electricity use. The data centre will require up to 1.2 gigawatts of electricity once fully operational, with 300 megawatts (MW) coming from the provincial power grid and 900 MWs from a dedicated, onsite bring-your-own-power scheme. The provincial Crown electric utility, SaskPower , currently has a mixed power generation portfolio of hydro, wind, solar, coal and natural gas. Most of its capacity comes from fossil fuels despite Saskatchewan having some of the country’s strongest wind and solar resources . Bell Canada says the facility will use a sealed, closed-loop water-cooling system paired with an air-cooled heat-rejection system. This system would not be connected to groundwater or the municipal water supply. However, that only accounts for the water used to operate the data centre itself. It does not include the water used by the electricity grid that provides power for the data centre. My dissertation research is focused on integrated water resource management in the Prairie Pothole region with a geographic focus on the Assiniboine River basin where this new data centre is located. Cooling data centres and power plants Dry cooling systems can expel heat; however, they require large fans and radiators to move heat into the environment and generally use more power. Wet cooling systems take advantage of water’s high latent heat of vaporization, much like our bodies do with sweating, to expel heat into the environment. Therefore, a reliable water source is required to continuously move water and the waste heat into the environment, much like how we need to drink water after sweating. Most electricity generation today remains highly water-intensive. According to SaskPower’s 2025-26 annual report , around 25 per cent of Saskatchewan’s power generation capacity comes from coal-fired plants. If the grid allocates 300 MW of power to Bell Canada’s data centre, cooling water will still need to be used elsewhere, far from the data centre. Saskatchewan’s current coal-powered plants use a combination of dry and wet cooling technologies. If built, small modular reactors located along the Rafferty Reservoir would require similar cooling techniques to operate. Read more: Are small nuclear reactors the solution to Canada’s net-zero ambitions? The provincial government has announced plans to refurbish and extend the life of three coal-fired power plants in southern Saskatchewan: Poplar River, Shand and Boundary Dam. Coal is planned as a bridge power source until planned nuclear reactors come online. Data centres might employ closed-loop cooling systems that reduce onsite water demand. However, that’s only one half of the water-accounting equation. To get a complete picture of their water use, data centres must factor in both onsite water use and the water used elsewhere to generate the power they need. Given the distance between Saskatchewan’s southern coal plants and the data centre near Regina, water demand will likely shift from one place to another . The total water withdrawn from the ecosystem may increase far from where the data centre is located. Using natural gas to power data centres If Saskatchewan follows Alberta’s path and uses natural gas to power data centres, it will take water to drill for, extract, process and deliver natural gas to customers. Saskatchewan has relatively little natural gas production . That means much of the natural gas will likely be imported from Alberta gas fields. The province can experience large seasonal swings in precipitation and temperatures. The amount of water entering supply reservoirs in the Assiniboine River basin can change on an annual basis. Yet, demand for water from industry, power generation, agriculture and municipalities isn’t always able to adapt to seasonal changes in river flows. Carefully managing water supplies will be an ongoing challenge in the region to settle this water balance discrepancy. More research will be needed to better understand changing flow-generating mechanisms in the region. In the Prairies, these mechanisms can include how water enters soils during the spring snowmelt or how wetlands fill up and subsequently spill into neighbouring streams. Authorities will need to consider the cumulative effects of increased water demand in the area, especially during prolonged droughts , to ensure they conserve finite water resources. Corwyn Shomachuk has received funding through NSERC Water Health CREATE, the NRCan Flood Hazard Identification and Mapping Program and the Manitoba Transportation and Infrastructure Research Grant. He is Board Director of the Canadian Water Resources Association, Saskatchewan Branch President of the Global Institute of Water Security Students and Young Researchers Association and a constituency association executive member of the Saskatchewan NDP.

articles.content: AI can improve our understanding of climate risks, but turning that knowledge into effective, equitable action will still depend on people and the decisions they are equipped to make. (Unsplash) Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan has described COP31, being hosted in his country, as the “ implementation COP ,” emphasizing the need to translate climate commitments into action. The urgency is mounting. In September, the latest United Nations Environment Programme report concluded that limiting global warming to 1.5 C, or even slightly exceeding that threshold, is no longer achievable . Although returning below 1.5 C later this century remains possible, it would require rapid, substantial emissions reductions. Meanwhile, continued warming increases the risks of severe and irreversible climate impacts, making effective action critical. Given this urgency, artificial intelligence (AI) is attracting attention for its potential to deepen our understanding of climate risks and inform our responses. This growing interest is reflected in COP31’s Antalya AI Pledge . But realizing this potential raises an important question: Do the professionals working on climate adaptation have the knowledge, skills and support to use these technologies effectively and responsibly? AI and climate monitoring A 2023 national survey of Canadian professionals found that many do not feel adequately equipped to apply adaptation tools or make the case for adaptation measures. This points to a gap between understanding climate risks and having the capabilities to address them. Canada’s National Adaptation Strategy sets a target for 70 per cent of relevant professionals to have these capabilities by 2027. Canada uses AI to improve weather forecasting , and Canadian researchers use it to assess flood risks . Emerging applications include infrastructure and adaptation planning, such as flood-risk modelling in Vancouver . Yet better information does not necessarily lead to better decisions. As AI enters climate risk assessment and adaptation planning, it adds to the challenges professionals already face as they grapple with difficult decisions about infrastructure, public safety, ecosystems and community resilience. Read more: Adaptation policies must be built around the local communities facing climate change AI skills for a climate workforce The challenge goes beyond learning to use AI. Front-line climate action professionals need to understand how AI-generated information is produced, assess its reliability and limitations, and decide when and how to use it alongside other evidence and knowledge. Consider a coastal community facing rising flood risk. AI-supported modelling might identify vulnerable roads, homes and public facilities. But deciding whether to reinforce a shoreline, restore wetlands, restrict development or consider relocation involves more than comparing projected risks. These choices affect livelihoods, ecosystems and relationships to place. They also involve competing priorities and values, Indigenous rights and jurisdiction and questions about whose knowledge informs decisions and who has the authority to act. Many of the competencies required to navigate these challenges are already recognized in climate adaptation practice. At the ResilienceByDesign Lab at Royal Roads University, we’ve developed a Climate Action Competency Framework that identifies systems thinking, critical assessment of information, collaboration, communication and ethical leadership as essential to effective climate action. These capabilities remain relevant as AI enters adaptation practice, but they are insufficient on their own. Professionals also need to understand how AI systems work, recognize potential biases and gaps in the data they use, assess the reliability of AI-generated recommendations and navigate questions of transparency and accountability. This does not mean every planner, engineer, emergency manager or public health professional needs to become an AI specialist. Instead, they need enough AI literacy to ask informed questions, recognize when additional expertise is required and exercise professional judgment rather than simply accepting what the AI produces. From competence to professional practice Identifying these capabilities is only part of the challenge. They must also be reflected in professional standards, education, ongoing training and the organizational conditions that shape adaptation decisions. The Professions Advancing Adaptation Competencies initiative offers a Canadian example. By examining how the Climate Action Competency Framework aligns with the standards and practices of engineering, planning, accounting and landscape architecture, the initiative identified shared competencies and profession-specific needs. AI can improve our understanding of climate risks, but turning that knowledge into effective action depends on people and the decisions they are equipped to make. (Unsplash) Similar work could examine how AI is reshaping adaptation practice across professions, what existing competencies remain relevant and where additional capabilities are needed. This would strengthen workforce readiness by identifying the competencies professionals need to use emerging technologies effectively, rather than assuming that access to AI alone will automatically improve climate action. If COP31 is to deliver on its promise to move from commitments to implementation, preparing the workforce responsible for adaptation must be a priority. Governments, professional associations and educators must ensure professionals have the competencies, resources and institutional support to use these technologies responsibly and translate climate knowledge into action. AI can improve our understanding of climate risks, but turning that knowledge into effective, equitable action will still depend on people and the decisions they are equipped to make. Robin Cox has previously received research funding from the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council of Canada and Natural Resources Canada.

Instead, they need enough AI literacy to ask informed questions, recognize when additional expertise is required and exercise professional judgment rather than simply accepting what the AI produces. From competence to professional practice Identifying these capabilities is only part of the challenge. They must also be reflected in professional standards, education, ongoing training and the organizational conditions that shape adaptation decisions. The Professions Advancing Adaptation Competencies initiative offers a Canadian example. By examining how the Climate Action Competency Framework aligns with the standards and practices of engineering, planning, accounting and landscape architecture, the initiative identified shared competencies and profession-specific needs. AI can improve our understanding of climate risks, but turning that knowledge into effective action depends on people and the decisions they are equipped to make. (Unsplash) Similar work could examine how AI is reshaping adaptation practice across professions, what existing competencies remain relevant and where additional capabilities are needed. This would strengthen workforce readiness by identifying the competencies professionals need to use emerging technologies effectively, rather than assuming that access to AI alone will automatically improve climate action. If COP31 is to deliver on its promise to move from commitments to implementation, preparing the workforce responsible for adaptation must be a priority. Governments, professional associations and educators must ensure professionals have the competencies, resources and institutional support to use these technologies responsibly and translate climate knowledge into action. AI can improve our understanding of climate risks, but turning that knowledge into effective, equitable action will still depend on people and the decisions they are equipped to make. articles.content: What would it mean to teach students who are learning academic writing to use AI in “ethical” ways — for example, large language model (LLM) chatbots like ChatGPT, a specific form of GenAI? In rhetoric and writing studies, guiding documents on the teaching of writing and literature caution against all-out bans and call for guidance on ethically incorporating LLMs into writing. My institution, the University of Victoria, is “ committed to support the use of AI in transparent, responsible, ethical and equitable ways .” In the context of teaching writing, “ethics” and AI tends to be shorthand for academic integrity, informed by questions about composing and authorship , transparency and the writing process . However, even when ethical guidance around AI use includes reflecting on when AI is appropriate at all, this often assumes, as a foregone conclusion, that ethical AI use is a possibility. AI has environmental costs , and raises profound social and human concerns . We are doing students learning academic writing a disservice if we don’t think more broadly about what “ethical” use means. Classrooms are political spaces Writing is inherently bound up with power, and many writing studies scholars and teachers see classrooms as inherently political spaces. They focus on practices that equip students to add their voices to academic conversations, without compromising their ways of knowing. For these scholars, classrooms are places to develop anti-racist , equitable and inclusive practices. Many encourage students to question power and privilege , especially in first-year writing classrooms. Students learn to build arguments, organize evidence and communicate effectively to specific audiences. They gain transferable skills and experiences that can be foundational for structuring the rest of post-secondary life. Read more: How a first-year university writing course for Indigenous students fostered skills and belonging Tyler Branson , a professor of literature who also teaches composition, describes how “we might be better off thinking of first-year writing as a course in the practice of citizenship” instead of a course in academic writing. He argues that “society needs students skilled in civic discourse now more than ever.” A larger sphere of ethical inquiry We should provide students with reasons for and opportunities to resist and refuse GenAI. In reasoning about this, I draw on my training in rhetoric to ask what rhetorical scholar Judy Z. Segal calls “prior questions:” Asking “what” and “why” rather than starting from the basis of “how.” As Segal explains, rather than asking, for example: “How to make cosmetic surgery safer?” we might ask “How and why it is possible that we see ourselves in need of improvement via cosmetic surgery in the first place”? Educators should be asking “prior questions” around ethical use of LLM chatbots. When we think about these “how” questions in relation to LLM chatbots and the first-year writing classroom — “How to teach students to engage with these ethically and responsibly?” — we need to step back and consider what “ethical” means. ‘Writing involves making ethical choices’ In the collection Naming What We Know: Threshold Concepts of Writing Studies , John Duffy , professor of English at the University of Notre Dame, contributes a short essay, “Writing Involves Making Ethical Choices.” According to Duffy, every time we write for another person, we’re proposing a relationship with the reader or readers. He’s particularly interested in ethical questions for writers such as: “What kind of person do I want to be? How should I treat others? How should I live my life?” With the prevalence of GenAI, how we choose to write, and not just to whom and about what, has become a site of ethical choices as well. What values are normalized? When educators in writing classes make choices about how to engage with LLM chatbots or other forms of GenAI, we must expand our ideas of ethics beyond authorship and academic integrity. We should also discuss environmental impacts, exploitative offshore labour and how the logic of economic markets is affecting key resource use (energy, water, land and minerals) and arguments for (and against) adoption. As media studies expert Kate Crawford reminds us, theories of AI must account for “the states and corporations that drive and dominate it, the extractive industries that leave an imprint on the planet, the mass capture of data and the profoundly unequal and increasingly exploitative labour practices that sustain it.” If educators default to “how” to use AI ethically in our classrooms, we bypass a more fundamental question of: “What makes us think this is ethical in the first place?” Expectations, habits, norms Drawing on the logic of “prior concerns,” educators should reflect on what values we encourage or normalize when we tell students that it’s OK to turn to ChatGPT and how these values could shape expectations, habits and norms. Research has shown, for example, that ChatGPT uses lavish, qualitative praise as a default setting . Will this instant feedback realistically prepare students for participating in human networks, including receiving feedback from teachers or peers? If writing instructors normalize turning to an LLM chatbot for discussion, we also risk normalizing students’ avoidance of the effort it takes to talk to someone at the writing centre, visit office hours or consult a librarian. The ‘AI refusal’ approach in writing studies One solution is turning to the “GenAI refusal” approach in writing studies . Writing studies scholars Jennifer Sano-Franchini, Megan McIntyre and Maggie Fernandes position refusal as a “ disciplinary and principled response ” to GenAI use in the writing classroom. They offer 10 reasons that refusal is a warranted response to GenAI. While each of these reasons is persuasive, I point to number 10: “Refusal can be a principled and pragmatic response to the incursion of GenAI technologies in college writing courses. ” Writing instructors are in a position to help our students think critically about what responsibilities we have to each other, the world and its future. As inherently political spaces, first-year writing courses in particular should provide students with reasons to resist and refuse GenAI, and opportunities to do so.
