articles.content: Tokyo then, St. John's now? A giant squid attacks a bait squid off the coast of Tokyo in 2006. (Tsunemi Kubodera/National Science Museum of Japan) , CC BY When I learned that Netflix planned to film the miniseries Below , about a sea monster terrorizing a Newfoundland outport , I thought to myself: “THIS I’ve gotta see!” First, the series showcases coastal Newfoundland, where I was raised and live. Second, I have studied ocean life in the island’s waters for most of my career. Third, it features the marine lab where I work , the Oceans Sciences Centre. And fourth, it stars a giant squid(-ish) animal (sorry Josh Hartnett). Giant squid have a special place in Newfoundland folklore and science, from early encounters with fishermen to some of the first scientific evidence of their existence. Unveiling the giant squid One key player in this history was the Irish clergyman Moses Harvey , who moved to Newfoundland in 1852 and undertook natural history research in what was then a British colony. Harvey’s research included revealing the existence of giant squid to the world based on a specimen that washed ashore. Fishermen had brought it to him to photograph and communicate to the science community in London. Arms, tentacles and head (buccal region, including beak visible) of a giant squid from Logy Bay, Newfoundland, photographed draped over Moses Harvey’s sponge bath in November 1873. (Variously attributed to John Maunder, Moses Harvey and Messrs. McKenny and Parsons) Fast forward to the 1960s, when the founding director of the Ocean Sciences Centre, Fred Aldrich , joined the faculty at Memorial University and soon focused his career on pursuing giant squid. Although Aldrich tried to catch a living specimen, he only obtained squid that washed up on beaches. Newfoundland is one of the global hotspots where giant squid appear more frequently, every 30 years or so (New Zealand is another, attesting to giant squid affinity for cooler waters). Below ‘s arrival roughly coincides with one of those cycles. The Rooms provincial museum in St. John’s displays a preserved version of one of these amazing animals. Giant squid: Not known to be vindictive Early in the series, we meet an (oddly) barefooted marine biologist walking through the hallways of the marine lab. This scene earned a loud “ewww” from my graduate students on the grounds of hygiene as well as occupational health and safety. The biologist turns out to be the expert on giant squid and the voice of sanity when fishermen, the military and a local developer all pursue the creature (nicknamed “Mudder” by the locals, foreshadowing why she is attacking the community) with bloodlust. This marine biologist also provides impromptu medical expertise when residents fall ill from drinking ice water tainted by the animal. (Side note, DO NOT entrust your local marine biologist with urgent medical needs — we are not that type of doctor!) I could join the Facebook crowd quibbling about who got the Newfoundland accents right and who missed the mark. Or I could ask why the Coast Guard would fully abandon people living on a small, isolated island in crisis. But Below generally did a good job on the science. The biology of the animal was reasonably plausible, including its swimming skills and even its ability to survive in ice. As a (likely necessary) stretch, I thought the intellectual prowess and directed vindictiveness of the squid in the series pushed the limits of credibility, although researchers have documented some impressive abilities in cephalopods (of which giant squid are members). Still, it was a good effort to maintain scientific plausibility and fun to see marine biota as the star attraction. Historical accuracy I took a course in marine invertebrates from Aldrich when I was an undergraduate in the early 1980s. Although he was in the late stages of his career, his enthusiasm for giant squid was still evident in his lectures. He would have loved to have seen the first live footage of giant squid in the wild collected just 20 years ago by Japanese scientists, and I think he would have enjoyed watching Below and he’d be happy I’m writing about it. I certainly enjoyed watching Below , not just because of the Newfoundland setting but because it seemed entirely appropriate for the story, which was in some ways a homage to Newfoundland and its ocean history. The plot weaved in the innate capacity of local fishers to adapt and work together to solve challenges (who can “put the arse back in a cat,” as locals would say). It addressed the collapse of the northern cod fishery that threw some 37,000 Newfoundlanders out of work. And it began with a striking scene about the government’s resettlement of more than 28,000 residents of many small coastal communities to larger centres in the 1950s and '60s. It also captured the general mistrust of government in outport communities. My CFA (come from away) graduate students also appreciated seeing the “Screeching In” ceremony , and the real sense of Newfoundland conveyed by the series. Read more: The trauma caused by resettlement in Newfoundland and Labrador must be acknowledged Stoking interest in the ocean I am not a particular fan of the horror genre, though I recognize its nod to productions from decades earlier when creatures emerged from the ocean depths to wreak havoc on an unsuspecting humanity (think Godzilla , Jaws , and Orca ). Though the genre isn’t for everyone, most people I asked said they enjoyed the series, and particularly the Newfoundland ambience. I also applaud the Below team for communicating the complexity of the ocean, and their efforts to capture the imagination and interest of the public with its many unknowns. The series also underscored the ongoing potential for ocean exploration. Scientists discover thousands of new marine species every year and could discover many more if there were more of us. Many of these discoveries come from the deep sea , where giant squid spend most of their time. Most new marine species are small animals, but, as scientists sample more ocean, a surprise discovery occasionally emerges not unlike the giant squid in Below . Perhaps given Below ’s success ( the No. 1 ranked show in Canada on Netflix the week after its release , with an 87 per cent Tomatometer on Rotten Tomatoes ), Hollywood might see some potential in telling exciting stories that bring the ocean into our living rooms. That focus could inspire a new generation of scientists. I can’t help thinking that watching Jaws and Orca when I was an impressionable teen helped to push my career interests towards the ocean, where my ancestors had also earned their living. Paul Snelgrove receives funding from the Natural Sciences and Engineering Council of Canada and the Canada First Research Excellence Fund.

articles.content: Imagine you are sitting on a train, moving at a constant speed. The blinds are drawn so you can’t tell you are moving. A light bulb hangs on a chain in the centre of the car. When someone turns it on, your human eye perceives the whole carriage lighting up. What actually happens is that light first reaches the two sides of the car simultaneously. A moment later, the light reaches the front and back of the car, again simultaneously. The light has travelled at the exact same speed in all four directions. Albert Einstein wondered how this situation would be described from the perspective of someone outside the train who was not moving with the car. For a drone hovering over the train, for example, the light still reaches the two sides simultaneously but the back of the car lights up before the front. This is because the train is moving forward, so in the moment it takes the light to travel to the front and back of the car, the back has moved closer to the light source and the front has moved further away. This phenomenon, discovered by Einstein in 1905 , is called the “relativity of simultaneity.” Physicist Brian Greene explains the concept of the relativity of simultaneity (World Science Festival). On the basis of this phenomenon, scientists have argued that in reality there is no objective “now” and that time does not truly pass. Some have even suggested that the apparent passage of time may be psychological . Modern cosmological observations, however, suggest that time is more than a mere illusion. The illusion of now Einstein himself declared time to be an illusion. On the passing of his friend and fellow physicist, Michele Besso, he wrote: “Now he has departed from this strange world a little ahead of me. That means nothing. People like us, who believe in physics, know that the distinction between past, present and future is only a stubbornly persistent illusion .” Along with Einstein, physicists and philosophers have often used relativity to argue there is no such thing as true simultaneity. For example, if you could say that a star several hundred light-years away is exploding “right now,” you could also stand up and walk away from it and just as well conclude that it won’t explode for another minute or so. By extension, if there is no objective now, and if all relative “nows” are on equal footing, then perhaps reality encompasses all of “ spacetime ” — every event that ever happens anywhere across the universe throughout all of eternity. Perhaps, as Einstein said, time really is nothing but a stubbornly persistent illusion. From the perspective of modern cosmology, however, it seems that an objective “now” does exist. Is the train really moving? It is tempting to say that the drone hovering in a fixed place above the train in our scenario is “at rest” and that the train is “really moving.” But we know the Earth is rapidly spinning and orbiting the Sun, which is orbiting the Milky Way, which is moving relative to nearby galaxies and so on. A composite image of the central region of our of the Milky Way galaxy using images from NASA’s Hubble Space Telescope, Spitzer Space Telescope and the Chandra X-ray Observatory. (NASA/JPL-Caltech/ESA/CXC/STScI) Therefore, neither drone nor train can be defined as “the one that’s moving” or “the one at rest” in any absolute sense. We could define either as an equally valid relative state of rest. On the other hand, if there was an absolute state of rest and an objectively well-defined “now,” we would require a concrete scientific measurement showing that the associated space has always persisted as such, along with a way to measure velocity through it from anywhere in the universe at any time. That would make the one state of rest objectively well-defined relative to all others. Such a space could then be said to “exist” in the usual sense of the word, with Earth and all of us existing in it, and it would provide consistent definitions of “now” and of “motion.” The cosmic now Cosmology delivers this. We have already made the required measurements using the cosmic microwave background (CMB) — the cooled remains of the first light released after the Big Bang. The CMB reveals that our universe — the three-dimensional expanding space where we live and evolve — has existed for approximately 13.8 billion years. It also shows the universe to have expanded by an integrated factor of about 1,100 since it formed; and that our solar system is moving through it with a velocity of 369.82 kilometres per second towards the Crater constellation . Albert Einstein was a German-born theoretical physicist. (Wikimedia) The integrated expansion of space throughout cosmic time has been so precise in every direction we look that across the sky we can measure “ anisotropies ” that were imprinted on the CMB at the time it was formed. These are tiny differences in the CMB’s temperature from one direction to another, of about one part in 100,000, which map the slightly denser and slightly thinner regions of the early universe. It would be impossible to see this if space were not objectively defined and expansion had been different here and there. This means that Einstein’s relativity of simultaneity still applies to local phenomena as a matter of relative perspective: neither the train nor the drone gets to say they are the one that is truly at rest, and both frames of reference can be used to describe reality, just as Einstein found. However, contrary to his belief, time is more than a mere illusion. The implication from modern cosmology is that the universe exists, and events happen all across space in the course of cosmic time. These events may be described as synchronous or not, depending on one’s motion through the universe, although there is in reality one cosmic time and an objective measure of simultaneity. Perhaps, as Einstein said, time really is nothing but a stubbornly persistent illusion. From the perspective of modern cosmology, however, it seems that an objective “now” does exist. Is the train really moving? It is tempting to say that the drone hovering in a fixed place above the train in our scenario is “at rest” and that the train is “really moving.” But we know the Earth is rapidly spinning and orbiting the Sun, which is orbiting the Milky Way, which is moving relative to nearby galaxies and so on. A composite image of the central region of our of the Milky Way galaxy using images from NASA’s Hubble Space Telescope, Spitzer Space Telescope and the Chandra X-ray Observatory. We could define either as an equally valid relative state of rest. On the other hand, if there was an absolute state of rest and an objectively well-defined “now,” we would require a concrete scientific measurement showing that the associated space has always persisted as such, along with a way to measure velocity through it from anywhere in the universe at any time. That would make the one state of rest objectively well-defined relative to all others. Such a space could then be said to “exist” in the usual sense of the word, with Earth and all of us existing in it, and it would provide consistent definitions of “now” and of “motion.” The cosmic now Cosmology delivers this. We have already made the required measurements using the cosmic microwave background (CMB) — the cooled remains of the first light released after the Big Bang. The CMB reveals that our universe — the three-dimensional expanding space where we live and evolve — has existed for approximately 13.8 billion years. It also shows the universe to have expanded by an integrated factor of about 1,100 since it formed; and that our solar system is moving through it with a velocity of 369.82 kilometres per second towards the Crater constellation . Albert Einstein was a German-born theoretical physicist. (Wikimedia) The integrated expansion of space throughout cosmic time has been so precise in every direction we look that across the sky we can measure “ anisotropies ” that were imprinted on the CMB at the time it was formed. These are tiny differences in the CMB’s temperature from one direction to another, of about one part in 100,000, which map the slightly denser and slightly thinner regions of the early universe. It would be impossible to see this if space were not objectively defined and expansion had been different here and there. This means that Einstein’s relativity of simultaneity still applies to local phenomena as a matter of relative perspective: neither the train nor the drone gets to say they are the one that is truly at rest, and both frames of reference can be used to describe reality, just as Einstein found. However, contrary to his belief, time is more than a mere illusion. The implication from modern cosmology is that the universe exists, and events happen all across space in the course of cosmic time. These events may be described as synchronous or not, depending on one’s motion through the universe, although there is in reality one cosmic time and an objective measure of simultaneity. articles.content: Some of the world’s most powerful technology executives are investing heavily in artificial intelligence while simultaneously preparing for the possibility that it could threaten humanity. From underground bunkers to isolated islands , some of the industry’s wealthiest figures appear to be making plans to shield themselves from the very risks associated with the technologies that their industry is helping to develop . The benefits of technological innovation are not necessarily shared by everyone, nor are its risks. Those who profit most from developing new technologies may not be the same people who bear the consequences when things go wrong. Sociologists have long studied this unequal relationship through the concept of “risk positions.” Just as people occupy different positions in society according to wealth and economic power, they also occupy different positions when it comes to risk . At one end of the spectrum are those who reap substantial benefits from producing risks while avoiding most of their consequences. At the other are those who benefit little from these activities but bear a disproportionate share of the costs . Who benefits and who pays? The economic rewards associated with producing risks can be enormous. Industries that generate environmental damage or financial instability , for example, can create substantial private wealth while imposing significant costs on society. Yet few industries have produced fortunes as extraordinary as the technology sector. Some of the fastest-growing companies in history have emerged from the tech sector, while their founders have accumulated astronomical levels of wealth . The prospect of accumulating even greater wealth creates a powerful incentive to keep developing risky technologies . But this is only half the story. To understand why risks may be produced beyond what is socially desirable, we also need to consider who pays for them. When those who produce risks do not bear their full costs, they have an economic incentive to keep producing them, even when the consequences for society are potentially devastating. The more effectively producers of risk can avoid these consequences, the greater the burden placed on everyone else. In this framework, it’s not enough for producers of risk to benefit from said risks; they also need to be able to avoid any potentially catastrophic consequences. They need to occupy the positions of “value skimmers” — those who benefit from upside of risk-taking while avoiding its potentially devastating downside. They are distinct from “value surfers” who gain from risks, but also bear the consequences when those risks materialize . Preparing to escape the consequences The distinction becomes particularly revealing when considering the growing tendency among tech executives to prepare for potential future catastrophes . Several prominent figures in the AI industry have publicly warned that advanced AI could pose an existential threat to humanity . Yet those warnings don’t seem to have slowed the development of AI at all . Locked in a battle for AI supremacy, there doesn’t appear to be an inch to give between competing tech giants . There are also concerns about generative AI that have come from within the industry itself. Employees and researchers working in the field have raised alarms about the scale and ambition of AI development, including comparisons to the Manhattan Project and technologies reminiscent of the fictional Terminators . Yet while some of the industry’s leaders appear to be doing their best to insulate themselves from these risks , their companies’ business models depend on expanding digital infrastructure and collecting as much data as possible. This expansion forces ordinary people to be constantly dependent on digital connection and leaves them fewer opportunities to avoid the risks associated. As AI becomes increasingly integrated into digital networks, those networks also become more vulnerable and risky. To prevent any aspect of our life from being outside internet dependence is to force us to be constantly at the mercy of technology companies. Could the public push back? German sociologist Ulrich Beck argued that modern society is one in which we must constantly face the social, political and economic problems of distributing a “poisoned cake.” His metaphor captured a central problem of what he called the “risk society” — the benefits of modern development are distributed unequally, while the dangers it creates can extend far beyond those who produce them. Yet Beck did not believe citizens would take this lying down. He argued they would come to see the reality of the risks being produced and act collectively to arrest control of this system away from those producing them. The conditions for such a moment may now be emerging. Protests against the expansion of data centres alongside parents’ demands that governments protect children from the harms of social media are just two trends that suggest people are coming to recognize their real risk positions. Perhaps people’s acceptance of bearing the brunt of the risks that they did not create is coming to an end. Whether it’s the people, the politicians or the tech giants who will win this debate is still to be decided. Dean Curran receives funding from the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council of Canada (SSHRC).

articles.content: When a human picks up a coffee cup, we use predictive processing based on our understanding of the world. For a robot, picking up a cup requires extensive training and simulation. (Unsplash) Today’s artificial intelligence technologies have become remarkably good at generating text and ideas that seem profoundly human. Chatbots powered by large language models such as ChatGPT, Claude, Google Gemini and Perplexity AI can write poems, brainstorm and find solutions to complex problems. The developers of these products drew heavily on the human brain for inspiration , creating artificial neural networks based on the workings of human neurons. Their systems now produce outputs that often resemble the outputs of human thinking. AI and the human mind, however, do not work the same way. Similar results do not necessarily mean similar processes. “World models” are an emerging technology that could help AI systems move closer to human “thinking” by helping them learn to anticipate what might happen and use that prediction to act. Still, AI will not perceive, learn or understand the world as humanity does. Read more: Cyber attacks? Bioterrorism? To ‘Pace the Frontier’ of AI effectively, we must improve our anticipatory thinking A falling cup, a complex prediction Imagine reaching for a cup at the edge of a counter. The cup may fall and smash if you misjudge the distance, grip it too loosely or move too quickly. For humans, grabbing a cup like this is routine. Yet this simple action relies on the complex ability to anticipate what might happen next. Our minds constantly try to stay one step ahead by understanding events and their causes. We can foresee the mess that would result from moving an overfilled cup or imagine a sofa getting stuck in a doorway even before we buy it. These predictions draw on expectations that form when we interact with the world . What we anticipate can, in turn, impact how we perceive the world and how we act. One influential family of theories, known as predictive processing , proposes that perception works partly in this way. The brain generates expectations, compares them to the information it receives and makes adjustments when the two don’t match. Let’s return to the example of the cup. Imagine reaching for an empty cup that you believe to be full. Your hand, expecting a heavier object, lifts it with more force than necessary. The cup rises abruptly and feels almost weightless. That mismatch provides feedback that helps correct the movement and update your estimate of its weight. What we anticipate shapes our actions, and what happens next updates our expectations. All this happens just to pick up a cup. Does AI predict differently? Even for today’s robots, reliably manipulating cups can require extensive training and simulation . The challenge involves learning how the physical world behaves and predicting the consequences of an action. Chatbots using large language models also make predictions, but of a different kind. They learn to predict the next word or fragment of text . This apparently simple way of predicting can nevertheless produce remarkably capable systems able to solve complex problems. Take the sentence: “A hand bumps a cup near the edge of a table. The cup…” Having learned patterns from enormous amounts of data, a chatbot might continue with “tips over the edge and falls to the floor.” It can do so by predicting patterns from a dataset and without ever physically handling a cup. However, being able to describe plausible outcomes does not necessarily mean a chatbot has learned why they happen . Teaching a robot to anticipate This is where world models kick in — a broad family of AI approaches that aim to predict how situations evolve and, in some cases, how actions may change them. These models can learn from videos, simulations or recordings of what robots see and do. For a domestic robot, this could mean anticipating that gripping too tightly might break the cup, or that a wrong movement could tip it over. By incorporating actions, motion and sensory information , preliminary research shows these systems can help connect predictions with what happens in the physical world. A world model could eventually make the same predictions we do about a cup. And as it learns from actions and sensory feedback, the resemblance to us may become increasingly hard to ignore. Still, arriving at the same prediction does not tell us what knowledge supports it or how that knowledge was acquired. Same prediction, same cognition? To us, a cup is not only a cylinder on a table. It can be graspable, breakable, yours, mine, too hot or almost falling. Our understanding connects the cup’s physical properties to a network of possible actions and consequences. Predicting that the cup will fall reveals only a small part of that understanding. And this understanding develops quite early. Studies suggest that infants just a few months old already have basic expectations about how physical objects behave . Child-development researcher Jean Piaget proposed that children build knowledge through acting on the world. As this knowledge develops, they become able to mentally anticipate consequences without having to carry out each action. For humans, learning involves more than accumulating information about cups. It involves connecting experiences when reaching for one, feeling its weight, seeing it spill and eventually imagining what might happen without even having to try it. Using world models, AI can also learn from actions and sensory feedback, in addition to videos, simulations and other data. Like humans, they can learn to interact with the world. The question is how their experiences contribute to the knowledge they build and use. AI could definitely come closer to anticipating what might happen and using that prediction to act. This alone, however, does not show that AI perceives, learns or understands the world as we do. As AI gets better at replicating the results of human cognition, distinguishing performance from process will only become more important. articles.content: Is that smoothie boosting your immune system or corporate profit? Research found over 96 per cent of immune-boosting content on Instagram to be from creators that sold or advertised products or services. (Unsplash) We all want a well-functioning immune system to help us fight invasive bacteria and viruses and recover faster from illness. Popular “immune-boosting” ideas, however, might be more of a hindrance than a help. Immune boosting is an online trend. Content producers share immune-boosting recipes — from smoothies to soups to poke bowls and pumpkin loaves . Nutrition books speak of “ super powered immunity ” while naturopathic clinics share immune-boosting “tips.” The “boosting” phrase has become so commonplace that it frequently appears in health content from reputable academic institutions . The COVID-19 pandemic — more so than ever in recent memory — had the public thinking hard about immunity . As interdisciplinary public health researchers studying the influential forces that shape public perceptions, the rise of immune-boosting discourse during this time caught our attention. We researched the trending concept in Google search results and on social media sites like Instagram . We found it to be problematic in two ways: First, content often presents scientific inaccuracies about how the immune system functions; second, it showcases corporations that push ineffective products or services. At a time when trust in evidence-based interventions like vaccines is on shaky ground , this can lead to negative outcomes for our health. Immunity and Society is a new series from The Conversation Canada that presents new vaccine discoveries and immune-based innovations that are changing how we understand and protect human health. Through a partnership with the Bridge Research Consortium , these articles — written by experts in Canada at the forefront of immunology, biomanufacturing, social science and humanities — explore the latest developments and their impacts. Balance, don’t supercharge Not all immunity-boosting content is inaccurate or harmful. Information from research or medical organizations often focuses on healthy eating, exercising , getting proper sleep and avoiding the harms of tobacco and alcohol . The idea of boosting or enhancing one’s immunity, however, remains fundamentally flawed. The immune system needs maintaining, not enhancing. That’s because each person’s immune system is complex, made up of cells, tissues, organs and proteins. This system works innately and non-specifically to keep harmful invader germs out, using, for example, the skin and mucous membranes as a protective barrier. It also works adaptively, deploying a targeted and specific response for harmful invaders. The body’s primary immune response. (Wikimedia Commons/Sciencia58) , CC BY-SA The adaptive immune system uses B-cells that produce antibodies — special proteins that attach to invader germs and either mark them for destruction or neutralize their effects. There are also T-cells, which act as destroyers, hunting and killing cells that have been infected by germs . Amazingly, the adaptive process of the immune system builds memory cells of the pathogens it battles. When the same invader re-enters the body, it can be quickly recognized and targeted more effectively. A well-functioning immune system also correctly differentiates between your own cells versus invader cells . An under-performing immune system increases the possibility and severity of infection . But an over-active immune system can lead to a host of autoimmune diseases like rheumatoid arthritis and multiple sclerosis. Maintaining the immune system therefore involves balance — not supercharging its functions and abilities. Corporations boost profits Those who promote the concept of “immune boosting” are often simply trying to generate profit. The very idea of “boosting” can create a sentiment of lacking — that one’s health could (always) be better. This frames health status as a deficit requiring people to continually pursue restorative or optimization efforts — a commonly used health and wellness marketing strategy . The first step is to establish a void, accompanied by anxiety or fear. The second step is to offer purchasable actions that address the void. Our research on Instagram during the pandemic, for example, found that more than 96 per cent of the immune-boosting content we reviewed came from creators that sold or advertised products or services. We found 62 different companies tagged in a sample of 28 posts. We also reflected on how the social media hashtag #immunebooster itself functioned as a rhetorical product used to “generate activity in the online attention economy .” Other companies may promote immunity-enhancing products or services with immunity-enhancing claims, such as hydrotherapy , IV drips, cleanses and detoxes . Cereal companies in the past have also marketed their products as “supporting” immunity . There is no good evidence that any of these activities have immune-function benefit. Stem-cell supplements Dietary supplements in the form of vitamins, minerals or herbs also offer limited benefit to those without diagnosed deficiencies. As noted in an immune-boosting article by a Canadian pharmaceutical chain, “to date, no drug, product or natural remedy has been officially approved by Health Canada to boost the immune system.” Yet corporations market them as either explicitly boosting or generally offering benefit to the immune system . Recent research from our team , for example, assessed the marketing of “stem cell” supplements on the e-commerce marketplace, Amazon. We found more than 40 per cent of the products claimed immunity-related benefits. Supplements are now big business, with a market valuation in the hundreds of billions . It is not surprising to find a broad, all-encompassing marketing approach to products such as “stem cell” supplements that have no clear evidence of efficacy for any health ailment Trust in medicine The commercialization of immunity is a concern for all of us. Commercialized health spaces , can damage trust in health-care systems and confusion around who and what we trust . If our perceptions are shaped by companies and influencers , this might negatively influence vital evidence-based health activities, such as vaccination. Rampant vaccine misinformation during the pandemic dissuaded vaccine uptake and helped promote inaccurate ideas of personal immunity . Vaccine hesitancy is highly complex, with multiple factors at play. Politics and polarization are increasingly influential forces . Inaccurate immunity discourse only further clouds information landscapes and, in turn, vaccination decision-making. Health and wellness marketing is savvy and alluring, carefully crafted to pique our interest and provide solutions. In today’s media environments, we all need to be cautious and critical of companies marketing products and services for our health and well-being. It matters when assessing preparedness for any future pandemic , and how our health-care systems can build and maintain public trust. Accurate understandings of immunity help us maintain well-functioning immune systems and a well-functioning society. Alessandro Marcon is affiliated with The Bridge Research Consortium (BRC) Jia Hu works at the BC Centre for Disease Control where his work is focused on on immunizations and vaccine-preventable diseases.

Commercialized health spaces , can damage trust in health-care systems and confusion around who and what we trust . If our perceptions are shaped by companies and influencers , this might negatively influence vital evidence-based health activities, such as vaccination. Rampant vaccine misinformation during the pandemic dissuaded vaccine uptake and helped promote inaccurate ideas of personal immunity . Vaccine hesitancy is highly complex, with multiple factors at play. Politics and polarization are increasingly influential forces . Inaccurate immunity discourse only further clouds information landscapes and, in turn, vaccination decision-making. Health and wellness marketing is savvy and alluring, carefully crafted to pique our interest and provide solutions. In today’s media environments, we all need to be cautious and critical of companies marketing products and services for our health and well-being. It matters when assessing preparedness for any future pandemic , and how our health-care systems can build and maintain public trust. Accurate understandings of immunity help us maintain well-functioning immune systems and a well-functioning society. articles.content: After decades of relative neglect, menopause is suddenly everywhere — in the news, on social media and in conversations among friends. Some are calling it the “meno-boom,” and booms attract business. The Canadian menopause wellness market — meaning the products, treatments and services designed and sold to help women manage symptoms before, during and after menopause — is projected to reach a revenue of US$784.9 million by 2030 . But alongside the marketing are sensational claims and outright misinformation , including about how the menopausal transition affects mental health. That’s exactly what my research team has been studying for more than a decade. And as a woman now navigating perimenopause myself, I have a personal appreciation for why these conversations matter. I’m far from being in a minority: the Canadian Institutes of Health Research estimates that about 10 million people in Canada are currently navigating some stage of perimenopause, menopause or post-menopause transition . So let’s cut through the noise. Here’s what the evidence actually says about menopause and mental health. Before you know you’re in perimenopause The increased risk of depressive mood arises early in what researchers call the early menopause transition. This stage is marked by menstrual cycles that are consistently seven days shorter or longer relative to a woman’s usual cycle. Someone whose cycle used to average 30 days, for example, might start having 23- or 37-day cycles. So unless you’re tracking your cycle very closely, it can be easy to miss any connection between mid-life mood changes and perimenopause. It also doesn’t help that depressive symptoms have been shown to fluctuate considerably in perimenopause, making it a moving target. Not just about depression and mood swings Though a lot of research on the menopause transition has focused on depressed mood, there’s growing recognition that other psychological symptoms can show up too. For example, a recent study by our team , following perimenopausal women for three months, found that more than half struggled with moderate-to-severe anger and irritability. Weekly changes in sleep quality, hot flash severity, as well as hormones, predicted weekly changes in anger. Estrogen fluctuation in perimenopause has also been associated with greater sensitivity to interpersonal rejection , highlighting that psychological changes in the menopause transition can involve more than just feeling down. This fits with anecdotes from women that say they just “don’t feel like themselves.” Read more: Perimenopause usually begins in your 40s. How do you know if it has started? Hot flashes don’t explain everything Hot flashes are no fun, and they are extremely common in mid-life, with 60 to 80 per cent of women experiencing them in the years leading up to and following their last menstrual period. But as much as hot flashes may negatively impact quality of life, they don’t fully account for the increase in low mood that we see in perimenopause. For one thing, the timing doesn’t line up . Across the population, mood symptoms begin to increase well before hot flashes emerge. And by the time hot flashes reach their peak severity, depressive symptoms are already declining. At an individual level, this translates to many women experiencing depressive mood in the absence of hot flashes and many others experiencing hot flashes in the absence of mood changes. Hormone therapy isn’t a cure-all Menopausal hormone therapy is highly effective in treating hot flashes and night sweats. Vaginal estrogen cream is also a safe and effective treatment for vaginal dryness and sexual difficulties at any age. The benefits for cognitive difficulties (memory and thinking), sleep and low mood are less well-established. Multiple rigorous trials have confirmed that menopausal hormone therapy doesn’t prevent cognitive decline. And though it has been shown to improve sleep difficulties in women experiencing night sweats, evidence for its benefits in women without these symptoms is less conclusive. As for mood, the overall benefits of menopausal hormone therapy have been found to be quite modest, although some women may benefit more than others. Cognitive behavioural therapy and serotonin-based antidepressants remain the first-line treatments for depressive symptoms, including during perimenopause. Future research may help us better pinpoint who stands to benefit most from hormone therapy. In the meantime, it’s worth keeping both its proven benefits and the limits of the current evidence in view. Not everyone struggles with the transition The increased attention paid to menopause and perimenopause is long overdue, and it stands to greatly improve mid-life care. Women should not have to suffer in silence or go untreated. But we should be mindful about how we discuss it. Women have long been dismissed as “hormonal” — meaning less logical, rational and level-headed than men. Careless narratives or conversations about menopause risk reinforcing that stereotype. Our research consistently finds enormous individual differences in how sensitive women are to the hormonal changes occurring in the menopause transition. For some, rapid shifts in hormone levels can trigger a host of negative mood symptoms. For others, the effects are negligible. Women experiencing difficult symptoms deserve recognition and effective treatment. But mid-life can also bring greater confidence, autonomy and opportunities for personal and professional growth. For some, menopause also means welcome freedom from menstruation and concerns about pregnancy. The “meno-boom” has brought perimenopause out of the shadows, and that’s worth celebrating. But attention isn’t the same as understanding. The research reveals that this period is more complicated (and more individual) than pop culture and business marketing can capture. Taking women’s mid-life mental health seriously means resisting easy answers. Jennifer L. Gordon receives funding from the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada (NSERC) and the Canadian Institutes of Health Research (CIHR).

articles.content: Police departments across the world use “sniffer dogs” to help in searches — for explosives, for people who are lost, for human remains and for narcotics. These dogs are widely understood as important for police investigations. They are often praised by courts for their accuracy and reliability. In Canada, police officers must have “reasonable and probable grounds” to search a home for evidence of a crime or to search a vehicle for drugs or other evidence during a traffic stop. In a series of cases, including R. v. Kang-Brown and R. v. Chehil , however, the Supreme Court of Canada has applied the lower standard of “reasonable suspicion” to sniffer dog searches. That’s because sniff searches are considered highly accurate and minimally intrusive to the individual searched. My recent research challenges both these assumptions. It suggests that the underlying rationale for the use of the reasonable suspicion standard in sniffer dog searches no longer holds . High rate of false alerts Despite our persistent belief in the “infallible” dog, empirical studies from around the world suggest that even trained and certified detection dogs have an alarmingly high rate of false alerts. In 2023, for example, data from New South Wales police in Australia revealed that nearly 75 per cent of searches following an alert from a sniffer dog yielded no illicit drugs . Similarly, a 2011 Chicago Tribune investigation found only 44 per cent of alerts led to the discovery of drugs or drug paraphernalia. This high rate of false alerts has multiple and overlapping causes. Poor and inconsistent training procedures can have a significant impact on field performance. A dog’s abilities also vary from day to day. In other cases, dogs are detecting minuscule residual traces of drugs on currency or alerting to the smell of drugs and not the drugs themselves. For example, the chemical compound piperonal is found in MDMA, but is also used in vanilla flavouring and mosquito repellent . Another source of error is handler cuing, or the conscious and unconscious cues a dog receives from its human handler. In a 2011 study , for example, dog handlers were told that markers placed in certain search areas indicated where target scents were located, even though no target scents were present. The dogs falsely alerted in 85 per cent of the searches and were more likely to alert at the marked locations, suggesting that handlers’ expectations influenced their dogs’ behaviour. Unconscious racial bias If a police officer harbours unconscious racial biases — even those they would consciously reject — they can transmit them to their dogs through unconscious handler cuing. If these cues cause the dog to falsely alert to the presence of narcotics, this will often give officers reasonable grounds to arrest the individual and, once the arrest is made, to conduct a more thorough search of the person and their immediate surroundings. The use of a reasonable suspicion standard makes it easier for police to conduct the initial sniff search, but the phenomenon of handler cuing operates just the same. This further reduces reliability and can lead to false alerts and unnecessary arrests. Moreover, investigations in the United States have found that police use sniffer dogs in stops involving racialized drivers at a disproportionately higher rate than stops involving white drivers. The 2011 Chicago Tribune investigation similarly found that the dogs’ overall success rate of 44 per cent fell to just 27 per cent when the driver stopped by the police was Latino. Physical and psychological harm Far from being “minimally intrusive,” the use of drug detection dogs can cause both physical and psychological harm . People subjected to a sniffer dog search often report feelings of fear and anxiety stemming from the public humiliation involved. Others describe physical distress, including increased heart rate, sweating and shaking. People who are subjected to a drug dog search also often report feeling uncomfortable in the presence of police and an increased fear of police afterwards. This can damage police-community relations, especially among racialized and marginalized populations where this relationship is often already strained. Reasonable and probable grounds The Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms does not prohibit the use of police sniffer dogs. However, my research suggests that the rationale for applying the reasonable suspicion standard — that sniff searches are highly accurate and minimally intrusive — no longer holds. Instead, the reasonable and probable grounds standard, which has generally been applied to search and seizure powers, should also be applied to sniffer dog searches to ensure that power is used in accordance with the Charter. If this standard creates a legislative gap that makes sniffer dogs a less useful investigative tool for police, that’s a matter for Parliament to address. Sara Gordon does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.content: In every culture, humans speak and sing to each other. We have created an astounding array of languages and musical structures across the globe. And yet, within this diversity, some fundamental sequence patterns are repeated. These are often referred to as “universal” patterns in human vocalization. Our new research, published this week in Science , reveals that many of these acoustic patterns in human song and speech are also shared with birdsong . The study compared the songs of 367 bird species with examples of song and speech from 52 human languages. How we gathered the data As researchers in animal behaviour and neuroscience and music, we ( Logan and Jon ) spent 10 years documenting the prevalence of universal human acoustic patterns in the songs of zebra finches . A zebra finch. (Unsplash/Angelo Casto) When Kendra joined our lab during her PhD , she proposed we investigate whether these patterns are shared across other bird species as well. To research this, we needed a large number of birdsong recordings. Luckily, many people around the world are fascinated by the sounds of birds and upload their recordings to public repositories . We collected and manually annotated individual syllables in the songs of over 360 bird species, generating more than 70,000 birdsong syllables for analysis. We then compared these to data sets of human speech and song from a variety of languages and cultures around the world . Fortunately, some of these data sets contain annotated recordings of the same individual producing both speech and song, which was perfect for our comparisons to bird vocalizations. Humans and birds both tend to end their phrases with longer syllable. (Unsplash) Regular and predictable rhythms Overall, we found numerous similarities in the acoustic patterns of bird songs and human vocalizations. For example, humans and birds both tend to end their phrases with longer syllables. Song of a fox sparrow. (Patrik Aberg) , CC BY-NC-SA 35 KB (download) They also organize their syllables in a way that minimizes changes of pitch across adjacent syllables. And they tend to produce their songs with regular and predictable rhythms. In some cases, birdsong appeared more similar to human song than human speech. In other cases, we found birds tended to have songs that were more similar to human speech than human song. Unrelated to vocal learning We designed this study to ask an important question: Does vocal learning ability shape sequence patterning? Humans learn the structure of their vocalizations from others, particularly as they grow up. It turns out many birds also learn their vocalizations as they grow up. We looked at two separate groups of these vocal learning birds: songbirds ( oscines ) and hummingbirds . We compared them to two closely related bird groups that are not vocal learners: suboscines and nightjars . Because humans, songbirds and hummingbirds are all vocal learners, we thought some patterns may be similar within these species and distinct from those within suboscines and nightjars. Surprisingly, we found very little evidence for this. The degree of variation across bird species did not appear to be related to vocal learning. Yellow-rumped warbler, an oscine songbird. (Unsplash) How humans and birds make sound What then might drive the similarities in sequence patterning across so many species? We will need more studies to determine the answer, but we hypothesize that similarities in how humans and birds produce sounds could shape some vocal sequence patterns. For example, the shared need to co-ordinate breathing with vocal musculature could contribute to shared acoustic patterning across birds and humans. Specifically, precise movement of muscles that control the vocal tract are timed with airflow from the lungs across all birds and humans. If this is true, it’s possible these patterns may be found in many other species. Did birds teach us to sing? Did birdsong influence the evolution of human sound? (Unsplash) Songbirds first evolved about 50 million years ago , long before the first lines of humans split from the other great apes. This means that birds have decorated our soundscapes throughout human evolution. The songs of birds have inspired music throughout time and cultures . Might these natural sounds have influenced the earliest humans as they began experimenting with making sounds themselves, discovering the joy of music to their ears? These are some of the big ideas we are excited to explore in future studies. Logan S. James receives funding from FRQNT. He is affiliated with Earth Species Project and Wavelength Science. Jon Sakata receives funding from NSERC, CIHR, and FRQNT. Kendra Oudyk currently receives funding from SSHRC and formerly received funding from FRQNT while working on this project.

articles.content: Cosmologists suggest that fluctuations of the quantum vacuum in the first moments of the universe played a role in the formation of galaxy clusters spanning the cosmos. Pictured here is the spiral galaxy NGC 2090, located in the constellation Columba. (ESA/Webb, NASA & CSA, A. Leroy) The word “vacuum” may conjure the image of empty space. Maybe you think of a region far outside the solar system without planets, debris, gas clouds or light. According to quantum theory, however, a vacuum is never truly empty . Quantum mechanics extends the Heisenberg uncertainty principle — which states that we cannot measure the position and the velocity of an object exactly at the same time — to a vacuum. The result is that a vacuum can never be still. Instead of an empty space, we can imagine the vacuum as a dynamic object, with regular fluctuations in energy. Physicists at the University of Cambridge in the United Kingdom recently presented preliminary research showing direct imaging of these fluctuations in a lab-made quantum vacuum . Physicists have “seen” the quantum vacuum many times before, however. And we can all see the effects of the quantum vacuum on atoms in the atmosphere — through the gorgeous light displays of the aurora borealis. The energy fluctuations of the quantum vacuum also create conditions for black holes to shrink. And modern cosmologists believe they played a role in the creation of galaxies, their impact felt in the earliest moments of our universe. Impacts on real objects The idea of a “quantum vacuum” that isn’t truly empty is more than an academic interpretation of equations. The most striking feature of the vacuum is the way it impacts the structure and dynamics of real objects . For instance, there is an ongoing effort geared at observing the quantum vacuum directly in an experiment using high-intensity laser beams . The strong electric fields from the laser pulses interact with the particles fluctuating in and out of the vacuum and, as a result, experience an effect called “birefringence.” The birefringent vacuum treats light of different polarizations differently, similar to how polarizing sunglasses preferentially block light from specific glare-producing sources. This complex and interesting experiment will test the predictions of quantum mechanics on the structure of the vacuum through direct observation. Changing colours of light This will not be the first time scientists have “seen” the quantum vacuum at work. By the mid-20th century, quantum mechanics had been put to test after test and was proving capable of predicting and describing the internal structure of molecules, atoms and nuclei. For theory and experiments to agree, however, scientists had to account for the impact of the quantum vacuum. In many cases, theoretical predictions were tested against the spectra of these objects found through experiments . For example, the electrons in oxygen atoms and nitrogen molecules have specific energy levels. The lowest energy level is the “ground” state, and the rest are “excited” states. Electrons can’t hang out in excited states forever. The quantum vacuum shakes and perturbs them until they fall back to the ground state. Transitions between levels are accompanied by emission of light with specific colours, dubbed the spectra. In the case of oxygen atoms and nitrogen molecules, this spectrum takes the form of dazzling display of greens, reds and violets in the aurora borealis . One of the specific predictions of quantum mechanics for the electron in the hydrogen atom is that the lower energy levels are particularly sensitive to quantum vacuum fluctuations. As the energy levels shift slightly, this changes the colour of the light that can be absorbed or emitted by the atom. This effect in hydrogen was precisely measured in 1947 by Willis Lamb who eventually won the Nobel prize in physics for what is now called the Lamb shift . Modern physics experiments The impact of vacuum fluctuations on the structure of particles and their interaction with the environment has since played an important part in modern physics experiments. The subfield of physics that connects the structure of atoms and molecules to the light they interact with is called atomic, molecular and optical (AMO) physics. I did my PhD in this area of physics, and those of us working in the lab rely on accurate calculation of spectra in order to use lasers to control quantum systems in neutral atom or trapped ion quantum computers and quantum simulators. Quantum computers harness “qubits,” a pair of energy levels analogous to the 0 and 1 making up a classical bit, to perform complex calculations. Quantum simulators, meanwhile, subject quantum particles like ultracold atoms to environments that make them emulate the behaviour of another system, such as a superconductor. Physicists must also take into account the direct impact of vacuum fluctuations on the basic properties of fundamental particles, such as the way in which electron-like particles called “muons” interact with magnetic fields , in order to describe what’s observed in experiments. Shrinking black holes A further interesting prediction of the quantum vacuum is how it behaves near extreme astrophysical objects, such as in the vicinity of a black hole. The first picture of a black hole was captured at the centre of the galaxy M87, using the Event Horizon Telescope. (Event Horizon Telescope Collaboration) The strong gravitational acceleration toward the black hole generated by space-time curvature modifies the number and distribution of particles occupying the vacuum. This causes the black hole to “evaporate” into the surrounding empty space . This is the only known mechanism by which black holes shrink and their contents, in some complex manner, escape from behind the event horizon. And this is enabled by the quantum vacuum. The dynamic quantum vacuum interacts with everything and has important effects, both observed and predicted, offering a fascinating history to reflect on and an exciting range of future experiments to look forward to. articles.content: A good and happy life is made in the small connections with others in our communities. (Unsplash) Earlier this year, we convened a meeting of some of the most influential figures in modern happiness research to discuss what they had learned in their 600 combined years of research and professional experience. The group included pioneers like Richard Layard , Sonja Lyubomirsky and Martin Seligman , who turned happiness into a serious science. As a result of their work, 90 per cent of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) member countries are now measuring life satisfaction. Many of these pioneers have remained active into their 80s and 90s, still writing , teaching and mentoring. If any group could identify the ingredients of a good life, this was it. We recently published the outcome of this discussion in the Journal of Happiness Studies . The group identified many central themes to happiness: having basic needs met, relationships, meaningful work and living in ways that align with one’s values and circumstances. Looking ahead, they were concerned about inequalities and declining youth well-being. The single most recurring theme in the discussion, however, was the importance and joy that comes from social relationships. Relationships are the linchpin As an interdisciplinary team of well-being researchers, we expected relationships to be part of the answer. They affect every aspect of life , amplify positive events , mitigate negative events and are considered to be a basic psychological need . This is not only observed in western countries; “having someone to count on” predicts life satisfaction around the world . In short, happy people have strong and satisfying relationships . What we did not expect was how frequently relationships would come up. In nearly every part of the discussion spanning meaning, work, competition, culture, morality, technology and longevity, relationships were the linchpin of happiness. Social engagement is a skill In their personal lives, several of these pioneers deliberately protected time for spouses, relatives, friends or grandchildren. One reorganized a schedule to give their close friendships more room. Another, persuaded by intervention studies , began writing more messages of gratitude , behaving more sociably and trading superficial exchanges for deeper conversations . Social engagement, they suggested, is not a luxury reserved for extroverts or the socially advantaged, but a skill anyone can cultivate . Connection may not always happen on its own, but it often begins with simple acts: taking an interest, reaching out and showing up. These are things we all can do. Their professional lives told the same story. Consistent with the research literature , many pioneers actively built laboratories, departments and collaborations where students and colleagues felt trusted, supported and energized. They saw people do better work when others helped them flourish and they helped others, discovering that others’ success and happiness could add to, rather than subtract from, their own. Relationships help healthier aging Happiness and relationships also offered a plausible link to the unusual longevity represented in the gathering. The scholars did not explicitly agree that their research might have extended their lives, or that any single practice explained their vitality. Still, their own priorities echoed a large body of research connecting close relationships with healthier, happier aging — a finding undeniably witnessed by the Harvard Study of Adult Development . The possibility lingered: Perhaps studying happiness had taught them to invest in the very bonds that helped keep them engaged in life? When the conversation widened from individuals to societies, the relational theme became more urgent. Several participants worried about declining youth well-being , which they attributed to increasingly competitive cultures. Schools rank students against classmates. Universities and workplaces turn peers into rivals. Material comparison makes another person’s gain feel like one’s own loss . Under those conditions, even talented young people can experience education not as discovery or fellowship, but as an effort to survive. Invest in the people around you The group did not deny that competition is part of human life or that it can sometimes spur innovation. But they challenged the assumption that self-interested rivalry is the key to progress. Human beings also survive and thrive through co-operation, social learning and mutual care. They argued that communities organized around a stronger sense of “we” are better positioned to flourish than those trapped in “us versus them.” This is consistent with research on the topic. The moral insight was simple: Your happiness is not my unhappiness. Your well-being can strengthen mine, just as mine can strengthen yours. We flourish by building one another up. The central conclusion was ancient enough to sound obvious but still not always easy to follow in our fast-paced society. A good and happy life is not constructed alone. It is made in the small connections with others in our daily lives, the workplaces we humanize, the rivalries we refuse, the communities we build and the society we all shape. After hundreds of years of combined research, the pioneers’ most compelling insight was simple: Invest in the people around you. The authors do not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and have disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.content: Every summer, Québec rivers increasingly reach water temperature levels that threaten Atlantic salmon ( Salmo salar ). Just a few extra degrees can make the difference between a favourable and hostile habitat for this iconic species. Because of climate change, the issue is no longer simply predicting how much rivers will warm, but determining where to take action to protect them. One possible solution is the reforestation of riparian zones , the edges of streams and rivers. Trees lining waterways provide shade, which limits sun exposure and keeps temperatures cooler. But how can we determine what areas will actually benefit from reforestation? Our study , conducted on the Dartmouth River in the Gaspé Peninsula — a major waterway in the region known for its Atlantic salmon population and recreational fishing — provides a new tool to answer this question. When water temperature is a problem A river’s water temperature depends on several factors including air temperature, flow rate and groundwater inflow. However, solar radiation remains one of the main sources of energy responsible for rivers warming during the summer. More sunlight reaches the water’s surface in areas where riparian vegetation has been degraded by human activities. The consequences of this are particularly significant for Atlantic salmon, a species adapted to cold waters. Atlantic salmon growth and performance are generally optimal at temperatures below 20°C, and signs of physiological stress appear when the water temperature exceeds 20–23°C. Beyond these critical thresholds, this stress can affect the growth, feeding, and reproduction of the species . Protecting thermal refuges has therefore become a major conservation topic. Mapping shaded areas To better understand the effect of riparian vegetation on water warming in the Dartmouth River, our research team at the INRS’ Eau Terre Environnement Research Centre launched a project funded by The Foundation for Conservation of Atlantic Salmon . The goal of this study was to assess the role of riparian vegetation in providing shade and controlling solar exposure — two key factors that determine the quality of salmon habitat. We used a remote sensing technology called LiDAR (Light Detection and Ranging), which produces a highly detailed three-dimensional representation of the terrain and surrounding vegetation. The analysis was conducted at a resolution of just one metre, allowing us to identify the most exposed sections of the watercourse with high precision. By combining LiDAR data with spatial modelling tools, we were able to simulate the amount of solar radiation reaching the surface of the Dartmouth River. We then compared these results with water temperature data. Shading varies The results showed that wide, sparsely shaded sections receive more solar energy, while areas that are steep-sided or bordered by dense vegetation are naturally protected. To take this further, we calculated an indicator called “unitary radiation,” which represents the amount of solar energy received within a given volume of water. This measure helps identify the areas most vulnerable to warming. We observed that certain narrow, shallow and sparsely shaded sections received up to 25 times more energy than other parts of the river. These areas appear to be particularly sensitive to summer heat waves. Reforesting riverbanks We then simulated a restoration scenario in which a 30-metre-wide riparian strip would be re-established with a tree canopy at least 12 metres high. This simulation was applied only to degraded sections of the river, where the loss of riparian vegetation limited natural shading. It therefore represents a realistic reforestation scenario that could be implemented as part of salmon habitat restoration projects. The results are encouraging. Reforestation leads to a widespread reduction in the amount of solar radiation absorbed by the water. In some areas, the reductions reach nearly 40 per cent. This reduction helps maintain cooler water temperatures, which is particularly beneficial for Atlantic salmon. Our study has identified certain river sections with a much higher potential for reducing solar radiation. It’s precisely these locations that should be prioritized during restoration efforts. Targeting investments more effectively The economic resources allocated to reforestation are limited. In a river system that spans hundreds of kilometres, it’s not possible to take action everywhere. Our study proposes a spatial prioritization method to identify the areas where every dollar invested in restoration could yield the greatest reductions in water temperature. On the Dartmouth River, these priority areas are concentrated mainly in the upstream sections as well as in certain tributaries, where the river connects to another watercourse that is particularly exposed. This approach could be applied to other watersheds in Québec to support conservation organizations, river managers and public decision-makers in their efforts to adapt to climate change. In Scotland , similar tools are already being used to identify river sections where tree planting offers the greatest potential for cooling the water and protecting Atlantic salmon in the face of global warming. A promising adaptation strategy Riparian reforestation is one of the concrete solutions that can be implemented locally as an adaptation measure starting today. By restoring the trees that line rivers, it’s possible to create more shade, protect thermal refuges and increase the resilience of Atlantic salmon habitat in the face of increasingly hot summers. At a time when every degree counts, trees could well become essential allies for the future of Québec’s salmon rivers. We would like to acknowledge the contribution of Mathias Cabal, a master’s student, as well as Professors Normand Bergeron and André St-Hilaire of the INRS’ Centre Eau Terre Environnement Research Centre, and Carole-Anne Gillis of the Gespe’gewa’gi Institute of Natural Understanding (GINU). Their expertise, collaboration, and commitment were essential to the completion of this research project. Eva Enders is a member of the Interuniversity Research Group in Limnology (GRIL), Résources Aquatiques Québec (RAQ), the Centre interuniversitaire de recherche sur le saumon atlantique (CIRSA), and the Atlantic Salmon Research Joint Venture (ASRJV). This research was supported by the Foundation for Conservation of Atlantic Salmon (FCAS) and the Alliance Advantage Program of the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada (NSERC). Nour El Houda Bejaoui is a member of the Interuniversity Research Group in Limnology (GRIL). She has received funding from the Foundation for Conservation of Atlantic Salmon.

articles.content: A Victorian-era séance. (Pearson's Magazine, 1910) In November 1857, during a séance in Jersey City, the medium Leah Brown claimed her body produced luminous particles . So intense was the luminosity emanating from her, she recalled in her memoir , that it almost burned her hands. She rinsed her hands under a tap and then pushed them into the damp earth outside. The following evening, luminous particles were discovered in the soil where she’d pressed her hands. They were later identified as phosphorous. In her memoir, Brown admitted to the presence of phosphorous but insisted her body had produced it. She further claimed that the manifestation of spirits in the body naturally produced “phosphoric lights” and the particles came naturally from her body. She added that mediums’ bodies could produce phosphorous and implied that they were part of what was then known as ectoplasmic remains — the viscous, gauze-like substance historically claimed by 19th- and 20th-century spiritualist mediums to exude from their bodies during trances. In truth? She’d probably secretly brought phosphorus with her and had used it in the séance. But her account shows how phosphorus was used in séances decades ago — and provides a glimpse of the chemistry behind making the dead seem visible as Halloween approaches. The dangers of phosphorous White phosphorus, also called yellow phosphorus, gives off a faint light as it slowly reacts with oxygen in the air. The effect is chemiluminescence, light from a chemical reaction — it’s not evidence of supernatural energy. In a dark room, the glow could indeed be rather uncanny and convincing of a phantom presence. Phosphorus is not a safe chemical. It’s toxic if swallowed and inhaling the fumes too can be harmful. It’s unclear whether those living in the Victorian era knew about these dangers or if they had any knowledge of the dangers of phosphorous. White phosphorous was used in “strike anywhere” matches , and many people — mostly women — working in factories where it was used developed a disease called phossy jaw . It affected teeth and jawbone. Certainly, long-term factory exposure is not comparable to séances, and we don’t have any definitive evidence of mediums suffering from this disease, but what’s relevant here is that white phosphorus was a known industrial poison and yet it was used regularly for seances. Nonetheless, a glowing ghost was not always a toxic ghost. In 1910, the magician William Marriott demonstrated how spirit hands could appear with some props and luminous paint. In 1877, William Henry Bailman’s luminous paint used calcium-sulphide and became a major commercial success. This compound could absorb light and glow in darkness . Ties between sciences and spiritualism Historian Richard Noakes’ work has shown physical sciences had a difficult yet symbiotic relation with spiritualism. Bailman’s paint is an example that ghost-making was part of a broader culture of chemical experimentation. In 1874, William Crookes, a renowned chemist, investigated self-luminous objects at séances. He specifically tested phosphorised oil and phosphorous lamps to see if he could understand the process better. Yet Crookes did not dismiss spiritualism as complete hoax. His writings suggest sciences and spiritualism were not completely separate worlds, and their methods sometimes overlapped. It’s important to examine the role literature played in understanding the link between phosphorus and ghosts. The most famous literary example of the use of phosphorus for ethereal spectacle comes from Arthur Conan Doyle’s The Hound of the Baskervilles , where the dog is treated with phosphorous to create the ghostly effect. Doyle’s work had profound impact on the development of forensics . The fictional use of phosphorous to create a spectral hound very likely brought more attention to the use of phosphorous within the spiritualist community. Ironically, the Scottish author had a keen interest in the paranormal and wanted to believe that ghosts existed. It’s strange how the creator of world’s most popular rational detective — Sherlock Holmes — was so deeply invested in the supernatural. Disposable bodies More recently, British author Laura Purcell’s Gothic novel, The Shape of Darkness , deals specifically with mediums and their use of phosphorus. Purcell’s novel is about a poor child medium who is unaware that the glow in her body is because of phosphorous and imagines that the burn she feels is because of the spirits. Her father is suffering from phossy jaw from his work at a match factory, and the book focuses on the inescapable nature of poverty and how the child is now the family’s only source of income. In both Purcell’s novel and The Hound of the Baskervilles , toxic phosphorous is used on subjects without any agency. The victims, a dog and a child, suffer health hazards just to create a supernatural phenomenon. Both these works of fiction give voice to a very real issue — some bodies have always been considered more disposable than others. Our Halloween decors today are filled with spooky things that glow. But once upon a time, a mysterious glow held the promise of extraordinary proof that the dead had returned for those gathered in darkness.
