articles.description: A Victorian-era séance. (Pearson's Magazine, 1910) In November 1857, during a séance in Jersey City, the medium Leah Brown claimed her body produced luminous particles . So intense was the luminosity emanating from her, she recalled in her memoir , that it almost burned her hands. She rinsed her hands under a tap and then pushed them into the damp earth outside. The following evening, luminous particles were discovered in the soil where she’d pressed her hands. They were later identified as phosphorous. In her memoir, Brown admitted to the presence of phosphorous but insisted her body had produced it. She further claimed that the manifestation of spirits in the body naturally produced “phosphoric lights” and the particles came naturally from her body. She added that mediums’ bodies could produce phosphorous and implied that they were part of what was then known as ectoplasmic remains — the viscous, gauze-like substance historically claimed by 19th- and 20th-century spiritualist mediums to exude from their bodies during trances. In truth? She’d probably secretly brought phosphorus with her and had used it in the séance. But her account shows how phosphorus was used in séances decades ago — and provides a glimpse of the chemistry behind making the dead seem visible as Halloween approaches. The dangers of phosphorous White phosphorus, also called yellow phosphorus, gives off a faint light as it slowly reacts with oxygen in the air. The effect is chemiluminescence, light from a chemical reaction — it’s not evidence of supernatural energy. In a dark room, the glow could indeed be rather uncanny and convincing of a phantom presence. Phosphorus is not a safe chemical. It’s toxic if swallowed and inhaling the fumes too can be harmful. It’s unclear whether those living in the Victorian era knew about these dangers or if they had any knowledge of the dangers of phosphorous. White phosphorous was used in “strike anywhere” matches , and many people — mostly women — working in factories where it was used developed a disease called phossy jaw . It affected teeth and jawbone. Certainly, long-term factory exposure is not comparable to séances, and we don’t have any definitive evidence of mediums suffering from this disease, but what’s relevant here is that white phosphorus was a known industrial poison and yet it was used regularly for seances. Nonetheless, a glowing ghost was not always a toxic ghost. In 1910, the magician William Marriott demonstrated how spirit hands could appear with some props and luminous paint. In 1877, William Henry Bailman’s luminous paint used calcium-sulphide and became a major commercial success. This compound could absorb light and glow in darkness . Ties between sciences and spiritualism Historian Richard Noakes’ work has shown physical sciences had a difficult yet symbiotic relation with spiritualism. Bailman’s paint is an example that ghost-making was part of a broader culture of chemical experimentation. In 1874, William Crookes, a renowned chemist, investigated self-luminous objects at séances. He specifically tested phosphorised oil and phosphorous lamps to see if he could understand the process better. Yet Crookes did not dismiss spiritualism as complete hoax. His writings suggest sciences and spiritualism were not completely separate worlds, and their methods sometimes overlapped. It’s important to examine the role literature played in understanding the link between phosphorus and ghosts. The most famous literary example of the use of phosphorus for ethereal spectacle comes from Arthur Conan Doyle’s The Hound of the Baskervilles , where the dog is treated with phosphorous to create the ghostly effect. Doyle’s work had profound impact on the development of forensics . The fictional use of phosphorous to create a spectral hound very likely brought more attention to the use of phosphorous within the spiritualist community. Ironically, the Scottish author had a keen interest in the paranormal and wanted to believe that ghosts existed. It’s strange how the creator of world’s most popular rational detective — Sherlock Holmes — was so deeply invested in the supernatural. Disposable bodies More recently, British author Laura Purcell’s Gothic novel, The Shape of Darkness , deals specifically with mediums and their use of phosphorus. Purcell’s novel is about a poor child medium who is unaware that the glow in her body is because of phosphorous and imagines that the burn she feels is because of the spirits. Her father is suffering from phossy jaw from his work at a match factory, and the book focuses on the inescapable nature of poverty and how the child is now the family’s only source of income. In both Purcell’s novel and The Hound of the Baskervilles , toxic phosphorous is used on subjects without any agency. The victims, a dog and a child, suffer health hazards just to create a supernatural phenomenon. Both these works of fiction give voice to a very real issue — some bodies have always been considered more disposable than others. Our Halloween decors today are filled with spooky things that glow. But once upon a time, a mysterious glow held the promise of extraordinary proof that the dead had returned for those gathered in darkness. Séances claimed to dissolve the boundaries between the dead and the living. And while we may continue debating whether ghosts are real, that spooky light in the dark decades ago was certainly not supernatural. articles.content: A new study with unprecedented access to Atlantic salmon farms in British Columbia raises urgent questions about the federal government’s approach to regulating salmon farms and highlights disease risk to wild salmon populations. The Broughton Aquaculture Transition Initiative — a multi-government agreement with the province and the Mamalilikulla , ’Na̱mǥis and Kwikwasut’inux̱w Haxwa’mis First Nations — enabled this rare access to salmon farms for scientists unaffiliated with the aquaculture industry. Read more: Learning from Indigenous knowledge holders on the state and future of wild Pacific salmon Scientists from the Pacific Salmon Foundation, Fisheries and Oceans Canada and the University of British Columbia repeatedly examined the open-net pen salmon farms over more than a year, finding outbreaks of the viral disease heart and skeletal muscle inflammation (HSMI) on most farms sampled. Three independent pathologists confirmed the diagnosis, and the First Nations subsequently removed the farms from their territories. As a viral ecologist at the University of British Columbia and as elected Chief Councillor of the ’Na̱mǥis First Nation, we participated in this research and are co-authors of the publication. Our findings suggest HSMI outbreaks are much more common on farms in B.C. than Fisheries and Oceans Canada reports. They raise questions about the federal government’s policy not to regulate piscine orthoreovirus (PRV) — the virus that causes HSMI — as a “disease agent” or cause of the disease. These findings also echo longstanding warnings about the government’s approach to salmon farming in B.C. , which prioritizes industry needs over risks to wild salmon. A history of government denial Heart and skeletal muscle inflammation gained notoriety in B.C. after researchers first documented the disease in farmed Atlantic salmon , and the virus that causes the disease was shown to spill over to wild salmon . Fisheries and Oceans Canada has repeatedly downplayed the significance of these findings , emphasizing uncertainty over whether the disease occurs in the region due to the application of diagnostic criteria more stringent than those applied in other salmon-farming regions. These criteria were developed by Fisheries and Oceans Canada alongside the aquaculture industry itself . The Broughton Aquaculture Transition Initiative program studies the presence of infectious agents in and around open-net fish farms. (Pacific Salmon Foundation) Fish farms heavily infected with pathogens Prior research has documented the consequences of fish farm diseases on wild fish. Farms are frequently infected with pathogens such as piscine orthoreovirus . These pathogens flow freely into the water and are transmitted to wild salmon . They have been associated with decreased survival and population declines in wild salmon . Fisheries and Oceans Canada’s assessment of diseases associated with fish farms deserves renewed scrutiny in light of these findings. The evidence that PRV should be regulated as a disease agent has become overwhelming, yet the department has not updated its policy since 2019, when it concluded that PRV is not an infectious disease agent . ‘Namgis First Nation initiated a judicial review of this policy in 2019, and then put the action on hold in 2021 as it appeared the federal government would follow up on its mandate to remove fish farms from British Columbia. In 2024, the First Nation reactivated the judicial review after losing faith in the government’s commitment to remove the farms. Independent scrutiny is crucial First Nations, independent scientists, non-governmental organizations and even Fisheries and Oceans Canada’s own scientists have repeatedly raised concerns about whether the department’s science advice is sufficiently independent from its policy mandate to promote and regulate aquaculture. Author Gideon Mordecai explains the risks of PRV from B.C. salmon farms to wild salmon. (UBC Faculty of Science) The way PRV is regulated exemplifies these issues and illustrates why independent scrutiny is crucial. Our study, combining Indigenous-led research and independent scientific assessment, has provided an important check on institutional assumptions. It will hopefully ensure that future decisions affecting wild salmon are grounded in transparent, evidence-based assessment of the risks. The federal government is currently stalling on its commitment to remove salmon farms from B.C. Whichever policy option the government ultimately chooses must be weighed against its potential risks and benefits — and that requires accurate information about the risks salmon farms pose to wild salmon. The contrast between the peer-reviewed literature and Fisheries and Oceans Canada’s own science advice demonstrates that the government is currently failing to provide decision-makers with an accurate assessment of those risks. Gideon Mordecai receives funding from the Sitka Foundation and Raincoast Research Society. He serves on the Board of Directors of Evidence for Democracy. Don Svanvik is the elected Chief councillor of the Namgis first Nation, which actively opposes open-net pen fish farms.

articles.content: AI adoption in medicine is accelerating: more than 12,000 primary care clinicians have enrolled in Canada Health Infoway’s national AI scribe program , about 5,000 Ontario physicians use AI scribes and roughly one in five Canadian physicians now use AI tools. Almost 60 per cent report a cut in administrative time. AI scribes are tools that, with the patient’s consent, listen to a clinical visit and automatically draft the physician’s notes. We’re writing as an emergency physician who has led digital transformation in emergency departments for six years and advises on AI readiness (Ali Abdalvand), and an organizational psychologist studying burnout and responsible AI adoption (Ehsan Etezad). Our observation is that AI keeps its narrow promise of saving time. But without proper frameworks, it quietly adds new burdens that absorb those savings. We believe the fix is organizational. Burnout stems from mismatches in workload, control, reward, community, fairness and values; not from any single task such as paperwork. One study found electronic health record design and use accounted for just 6.8 per cent of the differences in burnout between clinicians. When work conditions such as a chaotic atmosphere and lack of control over workload were also considered, that number rose to 36.2 per cent. In emergency medicine , physicians are interrupted 7.9 times an hour, and prescribing error rates nearly triple with interruptions. No scribe changes that. How AI quietly adds to physicians’ work I think we can all relate to the idea that when you complete one task efficiently and save some time, new demands fill the space, making it seem as though nothing was saved in the first place. But as AI introduces new ways of reducing the time physicians spend on documentation, it comes with novel ways of adding work, too. The time dividend gets spent. Saved time rarely comes back to clinicians. In Canada’s national AI scribe program , half of clinicians put the time they saved into other administrative work, and one in five used it to add appointments. Studies from the United States show the same pattern: AI scribe adopters across five health systems saved 13.4 minutes of daily EHR time and delivered 0.49 more visits per week. Errors do happen and patient safety is at stake. In two simulated tests , Ontario’s auditor general reported that most of the 20 government-approved AI scribes made errors. Twelve recorded the wrong drug, nine invented treatment steps and 17 missed key mental-health details in at least one test. The province says there are no known reports of patient harm. OntarioMD, a subsidiary of the Ontario Medical Association that helps physicians adopt digital health tools with funding from the Ontario Ministry of Health, responded that physicians “know they must review every clinical note generated by their AI scribe.” That safeguard is essential — and it is also work. Used to be authors and now editors. Automation often leaves humans the hardest job, which is watching for rare but serious errors. When physicians at one U.S. health system got AI-drafted replies to patient messages, replying time did not decline as physicians still have to edit the text to make sure it was accurate. More tools, more switching. In our experience, many AI tools sit outside core clinical systems. As an example, in one of our emergency departments, starting a night shift means logging into the work station, the health record, the dictation system, the imaging viewer, the EKG viewer and, most recently, an AI scribe; six systems before seeing the first patient, and a copy-and-paste at the end of every interaction because the scribe lives outside the chart. Thirty-nine per cent of Canadian physicians named better-connected, interoperable systems as a priority. Always learning because it’s always changing. Keeping up with constant learning is a job demand in its own right and it can wear people down. This is also known as AI fatigue , defined as the overwhelming pressure of keeping up with AI tools for people’s jobs. Change fatigue is a predictable response to how change is managed by the health-care system and health-care leaders and it is not a reflection of someone’s failing to learn or to adapt. A better way We propose a practical framework that can be used by health-care organizations to improve the adoption of AI. This framework, GRACE, was co-developed by one of the authors, Ehsan Etezad, and it sets out five principles for moving toward responsible adoption. GRACE framework for responsible adoption of AI. (Ehsan Etezad) , CC BY Govern adoption . Include front-line clinicians on AI committees. Give every pilot a stop-rule written in advance. If the pilot doesn’t return measurable time, or audits find errors above an agreed threshold, it ends or is redesigned. Respect autonomy . Keep use voluntary and let clinicians choose among vetted tools. Respecting autonomy is an essential component of responsible AI adoption. Advance access. Build tools into the core clinical record so no one has to copy and paste. Fund access fairly. Cultivate competence. Offer protected, paid learning time and peer “AI champions.” Evaluate effectiveness. Track burnout, after-hours work, note accuracy and whether time actually comes back. Another practical tool, the AI Adoption Matrix, maps organizations on two dimensions. Enablement is how broadly people can access, use and build skills with AI. Governance is how well policies, oversight and accountability work. We encourage health-care organizations to map themselves on this quadrant and work toward being “Responsible Pioneers” with GRACE. We encourage health-care organizations to map themselves on this quadrant. (Ehsan Etezad) , CC BY The real test There is increasing pressure to move fast with AI adoption in health-care systems and it will likely continue. We would like to clarify that we’re not arguing against adoption of AI in health care. We actually encourage it and are excited about the future it will bring to all of us. That said, we encourage health-care organizations to adopt AI responsibly because stakes are high in medicine and patient safety could be at risk. We believe success should be measured by how happy a physician can feel at their job and about their job, not just how many patients they can see in one shift. None of us wants our loved ones to be treated by an exhausted and overwhelmed physician, so let’s ask ourselves how can we reimagine a health-care system that won’t burn out our physicians. Ali Abdalvand is the chief medical officer for Elewana Advisory, a consulting firm specialized in health-care digital transformation. He is also a founding director of Western MedTech, a non-for-profit society focused on supporting health-care innovators. Ehsan Etezad provides private consulting at MEUS Science with a focus on Leadership & Culture, Responsible Adoption of AI, and Psychological Health & Safety.
